# Source file docs/en/roadmap.md

# Vela language roadmap

[**English**](roadmap.md) | [简体中文](../zh-CN/roadmap.md)


This checklist records implemented Vela language capabilities and remaining work.
Native AOT and JIT share the frontend, Typed IR, native generation,
and Isolate runtime.

## Language foundation

- [x] C/C++-style blocks and semicolons
- [x] `int` and `bool` values
- [x] Local declarations and assignment
- [x] `func`, postfix types, and local type inference
- [x] Integer arithmetic and equality comparison
- [x] Logical negation
- [x] `if` and `while`
- [x] Functions and direct function calls
- [x] Classes, fixed fields, and generated/explicit construction
- [x] Enums with explicitly qualified members (`Enum.member`)
- [x] Static type checking
- [x] Typed IR and shared native code generation
- [x] Isolate-local precise incremental mark-sweep GC

## P0: close the basic language loop

- [x] Add `<`, `<=`, `>`, and `>=`
- [x] Add `&&` and `||`
- [x] Add `for`
- [x] Add `break` and `continue`
- [x] Add `switch` and `case`
- [x] Add a `null` literal and nullability checks
- [x] Add `let`/`const` declarations and constant binding assignment checks
- [x] Define scope, shadowing, and declaration-before-use rules
- [x] Complete source locations and diagnostics for all parser and checker errors

P0 behavior is specified in [Basic language contracts](language_basics.md).

## P1: core values and object model

- [x] Implement IEEE 754 binary64 `double` values, operations, arrays, and output
- [x] Implement `string`, comparison, and concatenation
- [x] Collect strings with precise roots, field/array barriers, and accounted contiguous storage
- [x] Decode string escapes and Unicode escapes with invalid-input diagnostics
- [x] Define UTF-8 storage and code point length/index/slice units (no separate `char` type)
- [x] Add string-context primitive/null formatting and explicit primitive `toString()`
- [x] Add single-allocation array `.join(separator)`, string operations, and GC-owned `String`
- [x] Add Unicode code point iteration and grapheme cluster APIs
- [x] Implement explicit numeric conversions (implicit conversions are forbidden)
- [x] Implement invariant typed arrays, nested arrays, and compact contiguous storage
- [x] Add growable `T[]`, geometric capacity growth, reserve and insertion/removal APIs
- [x] Implement `Set<T>`
- [x] Implement `Map<K, V>`
- [x] Lower class methods to native code
- [x] Add `this` and `object.method()` calls
- [x] Define field default values and constructor initialization
- [x] Add static fields and static methods
- [x] Add visibility rules for public/private members
- [x] Add recursive function support and recursion diagnostics
- [x] Complete function types and closures

## P1: type system and pattern matching

- [x] Add enum `switch`
- [x] Add exhaustive matching
- [x] Add `match` expressions
- [x] Add type aliases
- [x] Add nullable types such as `T?`
- [x] Add generics such as `Set<T>` and `Map<K, V>`
- [x] Complete Dart-style generic bounds, declaration checking, bound-driven inference,
  and generic interfaces/methods while retaining Vela value types, container invariance,
  and monomorphization; see the [generic system contract](generics.md)
  for the full scope.
- [x] Add explicit interface / implements contracts
- [x] Add type tests and checked casts
- [x] Add checked dynamic values, heterogeneous containers, and dynamic dispatch ([design](json.md))
- [x] Diagnose unreachable statements
- [x] Require complete returns on every finite control-flow path

P1 contracts are specified in [Core language specification](core_language.md).

## P2: modules and standard library

- [x] Add `import`
- [x] Add `export`
- [x] Add module-level symbol isolation
- [x] Add import aliases for qualified access and name conflict resolution
- [x] Compile multiple source files as one program
- [x] Add console output
- [x] Add time, random, and math libraries
- [x] Add lightweight UTC calendar conversion and strict ISO date-time input/output ([contract](time.md))
- [x] Add basic string standard library APIs ([contracts](strings.md))
- [x] Add checked string numeric parsing with int/double parse and tryParse ([contract](numeric_parse.md))
- [x] Add Unicode string case conversion ([contract](string_case.md))
- [x] Add PCRE2-backed regular expressions with Dart-style APIs and typed matches ([contract](regexp.md))
- [x] Add collection standard library APIs
- [x] Add JSON parsing and serialization over native values ([design](json.md))
- [x] Rename standard class `Json` to `JSON` and add `JSON.parse<T>` / `JSON.safeParse<T>` with typed results, constructor-based decoding, and M0–M5 acceptance; passed on macOS arm64, with environment skips and platform scope recorded in the [design](typed_json.md#11-acceptance-scope)
- [x] Add fixed byte storage and typed byte views ([contract](byte_data.md))
- [x] Define process exit codes

## P2: errors and host integration

- [x] Add `try`, `catch`, and `finally`
- [x] Add `throw` and typed error values
- [x] Preserve versioned native source traces
- [x] Define compiler and runtime error formatting
- [x] Stabilize machine-readable runtime error codes independently of diagnostic wording
- [x] Add typed native function bindings
- [x] Define host handle rooting and lifetime APIs

## P2: performance and tooling

- [x] Typed native values and precise shadow roots for managed references
- [x] Per-instance constant pools and shared immutable code ownership
- [x] Constant folding, CFG liveness, dead-code and unreachable-block elimination
- [x] Jump threading, copy propagation and redundant-move elimination
- [x] Direct calls, field access and LLVM register allocation
- [x] Native frame/argument budgets and physical-stack protection
- [x] GC workloads and incremental pause-budget contracts ([GC](garbage_collection.md))
- [x] Native object caches with source rechecking ([cache](compilation_cache.md))
- [x] Source symbols, versioned stack traces and instruction inspection
- [x] Formatter, LSP diagnostics, highlighting and documentation generation
- [x] Native [debugger](debugger.md) and [JIT REPL](repl.md)

Current limits and ownership are defined in [native execution contracts](native_execution.md).
Async APIs and scheduling use the [shared runtime contract](async_tasks.md).

## Native execution and development tools

- [x] Native AOT synchronous, async, and dynamic execution, with `exe`, `obj`, and
  `staticlib` build interfaces ([contracts and distribution status](aot.md)).
- [x] Development JIT, Load, stateful Hot Reload, Reload through a new script
  Isolate, and optimized-frame recovery ([contract, Chinese](../zh-CN/hot_reload.md)).
- [x] Native class allocation elimination, path materialization, reloadable
  optimized-frame recovery, and private closed-AOT stack records
  ([contract, Chinese](../zh-CN/escape_analysis.md)).
- [x] Project configuration, source test runner, async assertions, mock generation,
  and interaction verification ([contract, Chinese](../zh-CN/testing.md)).

- [x] Map literals: completed M0–M5 in the
  [Map literal design (Chinese)](../zh-CN/destructuring_spread.md#9-实施阶段与验收).
  Destructuring and collection spread are deferred.

## Remaining implementation and acceptance

- [ ] Linux x64 and macOS arm64 AOT target support packages and clean-host release
  acceptance. A4/A5 remain incomplete; see [AOT completion criteria](aot.md#implementation-stages-and-completion-criteria).
- [ ] Linux x64 and macOS arm64 execution validation for JIT/hot reload and class
  escape optimization; see [hot reload validation (Chinese)](../zh-CN/hot_reload.md#13-验证与性能标准)
  and [escape analysis validation (Chinese)](../zh-CN/escape_analysis.md#9-验证与性能证据).
- [ ] JIT performance approaching closed AOT; current measurements do not meet
  that goal. See [performance evidence (Chinese)](../zh-CN/hot_reload.md#13-验证与性能标准).
- [ ] Dedicated VS Code test-panel UI integration; see
  [testing tool contracts (Chinese)](../zh-CN/testing.md#9-报告与工具链).

Console input is outside the current standard API; see [standard library scope](standard_library.md).

# Source file docs/en/language_basics.md

# Basic language contracts

[**English**](language_basics.md) | [简体中文](../zh-CN/language_basics.md)


This document defines the P0 control-flow, nullability, scope, and diagnostic
contracts. Numeric conversions remain explicit; `int` and `double` do not mix.

## Switch statements

```typescript
switch (value) {
  case 0:
  case 1:
    print("small");
    break;
  default:
    print("other");
}
```

The selector is evaluated exactly once. Its type must be non-nullable `int`,
`bool`, `string`, or an enum. Case labels must have that exact type and be
compile-time constants. Supported constants include literals, explicitly
qualified enum members, earlier `const` bindings with constant initializers,
and supported unary/binary constant expressions. Calls, mutable bindings,
overflow, and division by zero cannot produce case constants. Duplicate case
values and multiple defaults are errors.

Empty labels share the following statements. A non-empty branch with a path
into the next label is a compile-time error; use `break`, `continue`, `return`,
`throw`, or control flow that exits on every path. The final branch may finish
normally. A default may appear anywhere and follows the same rule; it is entered
only when no case matches. An empty switch still evaluates its selector.

`break` exits the nearest loop or switch. `continue` targets the nearest loop,
passing through enclosing switches; in a `for` loop it executes the increment.
Each case body has a separate lexical scope, so entering a later case cannot
observe uninitialized declarations from an earlier case. Use an outer binding
to share state between branches.

Return analysis composes fallthrough branches from last to first, consumes
switch breaks, and preserves loop continues. Without a default, an unmatched
selector remains a fallthrough path. Exhaustive `match` expressions are a
separate construct; see [P1 matching contracts](core_language.md#normal-enums-and-exhaustive-match-expressions).

Lowering retains typed comparisons and jumps for dispatch; native optimization
selects the final machine representation, including table-based forms where
applicable. Labels have no runtime evaluation or allocation. Native frame and
argument budgets are defined in [execution contracts](native_execution.md).

## Nullable types

`T?` contains exactly the values of `T` plus `null`. `T` may be assigned to
`T?` without changing its representation or value. This is type widening;
it does not allow numeric conversion or a different underlying type.
`null` cannot initialize or be returned as a non-nullable type.
The `?` suffix describes the type, not whether a variable, field, or argument
may be omitted. Local declarations still require initializers.

```typescript
func read(value: int?): int {
  if (value == null) return 0;
  return value + 1;
}
```

Nullable parameters, locals, returns, class fields, and array elements are
supported. `void?` and repeated `?` suffixes are errors. A bare null initializer
requires an explicit nullable annotation. Array suffixes bind in source order:

| Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `int?[]` | Non-nullable array of nullable integers |
| `int[]?` | Nullable array of non-nullable integers |
| `int?[]?` | Nullable array of nullable integers |

Array element types remain invariant: an existing `int[]` is not an `int?[]`.
An array literal may use its expected element type, including null elements.

Non-null checks promote local variables and parameters on applicable paths.
The analysis understands `== null`, `!= null`, operand reversal, logical
negation, short-circuit `&&`/`||`, and guard returns. Local `let` and `const`
initializers follow the same rule as later assignments: a statically non-null
value establishes a non-null fact; a nullable or dynamic value cannot prove it.
An assignment replaces the previous fact. Calls that may modify a captured mutable
local invalidate its fact. Promotion does not change the declared type, so an
`int?` local can still be assigned null and can still use `??`.
Branches intersect facts at joins. Loops and switches conservatively discard
facts for locals they may write. Loop backedges and continue paths cannot
reuse a fact that a previous iteration could invalidate.

```typescript
func main(): void {
  let value: int? = 3;
  print(value + 1); // 4: the initializer proves value is non-null.
  value = null;
  // print(value + 1); // Error: value may be null.
}
```

Using an operand that may be null in numeric arithmetic, ordering, bitwise
operations, or boolean conditions reports the operand and requests a null check.
String concatenation and interpolation still format nullable primitive values
under the [string-context rules](strings.md).

Conditional expressions check each arm with its condition's facts and merge
only facts shared by both arms. A write in one arm does not affect checking
the other arm; for example, `value != null ? value.length : 0` is valid.

Fields and indexed elements are not promoted because another operation may
change their contents. For a non-null value, copy the value to a local and check
it, or use null-safe operators: `?.` skips member access or a method call when
the receiver is null, and `?.[index]` also skips evaluation of the index when
the array is null.

`left ?? right` evaluates the left operand once and evaluates the right operand
only when the left result is null. It returns the selected value without
assigning to the left variable, field, or array element. `??=` is not supported;
writing the result back requires explicit assignment.

```typescript
let value: int? = null;
const result: int = value ?? 42; // result is 42; value remains null.
```

Null comparisons are allowed for value types. Equality of nullable values
requires the same underlying type; null equals only null. Non-null strings
compare by contents, primitives by their existing typed equality, and class
objects, `Map<K, V>`, and `Set<T>` by identity. Array and builder equality remain
undefined except for comparison with null.

Statically typed Map/Set `==` and `!=` require matching collection kinds and type arguments;
either operand may be nullable. Separately created collections remain unequal
even when their contents match. Mutating a collection does not change its identity.
JIT and AOT compare statically typed collection pointers directly, including
nullable references, without traversal or allocation, in O(1) time.
Comparisons through `dynamic` use the same identity semantics through the existing
dynamic operation's value-kind checks.

Registers and fields already store tagged `Value` slots, so nullable values
need no wrapper object. Nullable primitive arrays use contiguous `Value`
slots. Nullable reference arrays retain pointer-sized elements, using a null
pointer for null. Non-nullable primitive arrays retain compact native storage.
GC scans reference arrays and applies their existing write barriers.

## Scope and declaration order

Top-level types, function signatures, fields, and method signatures are
collected before function bodies. They may refer to later declarations,
including mutually recursive functions. Type/function name collisions are
errors. Field and method names cannot collide within a class.

Local bindings become visible after their initializer is checked. Initializers
may refer to an existing outer binding of the same name; self-reference without
an outer binding is an unknown-name error. Locals must be declared before use.
Duplicates in one scope are errors. Function parameters and the outer function
body share a scope, so the body cannot redeclare a parameter.

Nested blocks may shadow outer bindings. Locals also take precedence over
global function, constructor, and enum names; a local value cannot be called
as a function. `this` is reserved for the constant method receiver and cannot
be declared or shadowed explicitly. `const` prevents rebinding, not mutation
through object or array references.

An `if` branch or loop body has a local scope even without braces. A `for`
initializer is visible to its condition, body, and increment, but not after
the loop. Each case has its own scope as described above.

## Diagnostic locations

Lexer tokens, AST nodes, and IR instructions carry a compact source ID and
one-based line/column. Columns count UTF-8 bytes; tabs count as one byte, and
LF advances the line. CRLF source also advances once per LF. Filenames are
stored once in the program rather than copied into every AST node.

Diagnostics own their source path, so results survive destruction of the parsed
program. File checking and compilation report the actual imported file for
syntax and type errors. Import resolution failures point to the importing
string literal. In-memory multi-source compilation uses `<source:1>`,
`<source:2>`, etc. Single unnamed sources retain line/column without a path.
The CLI renders `path:line:column: error: message`.

Duplicate declarations point to the repeated declaration token; duplicate
enum members retain their individual location. Unterminated block comments
point to their opening delimiter. Parser recovery preserves closing braces
and the following top-level declaration after an incomplete function body.

# Source file docs/en/core_language.md

# Core language specification

[**English**](core_language.md) | [简体中文](../zh-CN/core_language.md)


This document defines the core language features, object model, and runtime contracts for Vela.
Function type annotations contain only parameter types, followed by `=>` and
the return type; parameter names remain in function declarations and lambdas.
Runnable versions are in [`examples/`](../../examples/).
`func`, postfix annotations, strict types, explicit
enum qualification, and `T?` remain established rules. Switch labels may share
an empty branch; a non-empty branch must not fall through to another label.

Explicit `dynamic` values retain their actual language type, including null.
Operations and conversions to concrete types are checked at runtime. Containers
keep their declared type arguments when erased to dynamic; `int[]` does not become
`dynamic[]`. See [JSON and dynamic values](json.md) for the complete contract and
[`examples/json.vela`](../../examples/json.vela) for parsing and model serialization.

## Integer literals

Integer literals use decimal digits by default. The prefixes `0x` / `0X`,
`0b` / `0B`, and `0o` / `0O` select hexadecimal, binary, and octal respectively:
`0x2a`, `0b101010`, and `0o52` all have type `int` and value 42. Hexadecimal
digits are case-insensitive. A leading zero alone does not select octal: `052`
is decimal 52.

Every prefix requires at least one digit valid for its radix. Digit separators,
suffixes, and non-decimal floating-point literals are not supported. All forms
use the same signed 64-bit range, `[-2^63, 2^63 - 1]`; for example,
`-0x8000000000000000` is valid, while positive `0x8000000000000000` is out of
range. Non-decimal literals do not reinterpret an unsigned bit pattern as a
negative integer. Formatting preserves the original prefix and digit spelling;
ordinary integer string output remains decimal.

## Functions, function values, and closures

Script functions, methods, lambdas, and explicit constructors can declare parameter defaults:

```vela
func update(action: (() => void)? = null): void {
  if (action != null) { action(); }
}
func updateDemo(): void {
  update();
  update((): void => { print('updated'); });
}
```

Defaults run only for omitted arguments; passing `null` explicitly does not select a default.
Supplied arguments run in source order first, followed by omitted defaults in parameter order.
Defaults may reference earlier parameters and their lexical environment. Instance-method defaults
may use `this`; constructor defaults cannot access the object being built. External declarations
and accessors do not accept parameter defaults. Interface implementations and overrides preserve
which parameters have defaults; virtual calls use the selected implementation's default expressions.

```typescript
func add(left: int, right: int): int {
  return left + right;
}

func apply(value: int, operation: (int) => int): int {
  return operation(value);
}

func makeCounter(start: int): () => int {
  let current: int = start;
  return (): int => {
    current = current + 1;
    return current;
  };
}

func functionDemo(): void {
  const operation: (int, int) => int = add;
  print(operation(20, 22));             // 42

  const twice: (int) => int = value => value * 2;
  print(apply(21, twice));              // 42

  const counter: () => int = makeCounter(40);
  print(counter());                     // 41
  print(counter());                     // 42
}
```

Function types list parameter types in order without parameter names, such as
`(int, int) => int`. Calls through these types use positional arguments.
Function declarations and lambdas still declare named parameters. Lambda
annotations can be inferred from their expected function type, such as
`const twice: (int) => int = value => value * 2`. Without parameter context,
`(value: int) => value * 2` infers its return type from the body. See
[type inference](type_inference.md) for the shared rules and diagnostics.
Lambdas use `=>`; both expression and
block bodies are supported. Parameters and return types remain explicit in
function declarations. Captures use lexical bindings: mutation of a captured `let` is
shared, and its lifetime extends beyond the defining call. Capturing a `const`
does not make its referenced object immutable.

Use inference or an alias to avoid repeating a long function type:

```typescript
type BinaryOperation = (int, int) => int;

func aliasDemo(): void {
  const operation: BinaryOperation = add;
  const inferred = add;
  print(operation(20, 22));             // 42
  print(inferred(20, 22));              // 42
}
```

Instance method values retain their receiver, evaluated once when the value is
created. This includes primitive, string, builder, array, and collection
builtins, inherited methods, and interface/super bindings. A null-safe method
access returns null for a null receiver; a live binding keeps its receiver alive.

```vela
func builtinValues(): void {
  const values = [20, 22];
  const copy: () => int[] = values.slice;
  const append: (int) => int = values.push;
  const map: ((int) => string) => string[] = values.map;
  append(42);
  print(copy().length); // 3
  print(map(value => value.toString()).join(',')); // 20,22,42
}
```

A function value has a fixed positional signature. A contextual function type
can omit trailing defaulted script parameters, selects a legal argument count for
optional/variadic builtin methods, and fixes
callback/result types for higher-order methods. Without such context, an ordinary
fixed-parameter builtin value uses its complete parameter list; variadic and
callback algorithm values require a function type context. For example, inferred
`values.slice` takes two indices, while the annotated copy above takes none.
Defaults are evaluated by the underlying method at invocation, not at binding.

A class name can be used as a constructor function value. Its contextual function type selects
the arguments supplied to the ordinary constructor. Generated field constructors map positional
function arguments to their declared parameter names; omitted arguments retain their defaults.
Access checks and generic inference follow direct construction. Without a function type context,
the value uses the constructor's complete parameter list.

```vela
class Counter { value: int = 42; }
func create(factory: () => Counter): Counter { return factory(); }
func constructorDemo(): void {
  const counter = create(Counter);
  const withValue: (int) => Counter = Counter;
  print(counter.value + withValue(0).value); // 42
}
```

## Generic functions, classes, interfaces, methods, and aliases

```typescript
type UserId = int;
type IntOperation = (int) => int;

func identity<T>(value: T): T {
  return value;
}

class Box<T> {
  value: T;

  get(): T {
    return this.value;
  }
}

func genericDemo(): void {
  const id: UserId = identity<int>(42);
  const box: Box<int> = Box<int>(value: id);
  print(box.get());                     // 42
}
```

Aliases are transparent names, not distinct nominal types. Calls, construction,
and function values with a function type context may infer type arguments under
the [shared inference rules](type_inference.md); type annotations remain complete.
The compiler specializes static generic uses,
preserving primitive storage instead of boxing every `T` as a heap object.
Equivalent transparent aliases and equal explicit/inferred applications reuse
the same specialization. Functions, classes, interfaces, aliases, and instance/static
methods can declare parameters; owner and method parameters have distinct identities.

Each parameter may have one `extends` bound. Bounds can reference other parameters,
including later ones, and support recursive constraints such as
`T extends Comparable<T>`. Every loaded definition must be valid even when unused.
Unbounded T has no arbitrary members, and a bound does not authorize `T()` construction.
Dynamic and nullable values cannot prove a non-null bound. Generic implementations
and overrides must have equivalent parameter counts, normalized bounds, and
signatures after parameter renaming. See [generics](generics.md) for the complete rules.

Independent specializations have
no fixed count limit. Generic dependency expansion and type nesting are each
bounded to 128 levels; exceeding either produces a diagnostic. Dependencies are
expanded depth first so branching recursive templates reach that boundary
without first generating an exponentially wide work queue.

## Interfaces and explicit implementation

```typescript
interface Measurable {
  measure(): int;
}

class Rectangle implements Measurable {
  width: int;
  height: int;

  measure(): int {
    return this.width * this.height;
  }
}

func area(value: Measurable): int {
  return value.measure();
}

func interfaceDemo(): void {
  const rectangle: Rectangle = Rectangle(width: 6, height: 7);
  print(area(rectangle));               // 42

  const measure: () => int = rectangle.measure;
  print(measure());                     // 42
}
```

`implements` must be declared; matching method names alone do not implement an
interface. Signatures must agree without numeric conversion. Using an object
as an interface preserves its identity and numeric representation. Ordinary public
instance methods dispatch to the most specific implementation for the actual receiver,
whether the receiver's static type is a class or an interface. The static type controls
member visibility and signature checking. Calls through `this` inside a base method,
generic instance methods, and explicit getters/setters follow the same rule. Overrides
require `override` and must preserve the signature contract. `super.method()` explicitly
selects an implementation along the lexical parent chain while retaining the current
receiver. Private methods, static methods, constructors, and top-level functions do not
participate in instance virtual dispatch. An `is` test refines static type information
without changing dispatch. Extracted method values bind their receiver and the
implementation selected when the value is created.

```typescript
class Component {
  build(): int { return 0; }
  render(): int { return this.build(); }
}
class Button extends Component {
  override build(): int { return 42; }
}
func renderComponent(value: Component): int { return value.render(); }
// renderComponent(Button()) returns 42: the base method calls Button.build().
```

## Normal enums and exhaustive match expressions

```typescript
enum Brightness {
  light,
  dark,
}

func brightnessName(value: Brightness): string {
  return match (value) {
    Brightness.light => "light",
    Brightness.dark => "dark",
  };
}

func nullableValue(value: int?): int {
  return match (value) {
    null => 0,
    let present => present,
  };
}

func enumDemo(): void {
  print(brightnessName(Brightness.light)); // light
}
```

Match evaluates its selector once and chooses one arm, without fallthrough.
Every possible value must be covered; missing enum variants are compile errors.
`let` binds the selected value; `_` is a wildcard. Arms must produce the same type, apart
from the existing permitted nullable widening. A selector covering all non-null
values followed by a null arm, or vice versa, supports nullable narrowing.
The catch-all `let present` above excludes null after the preceding null arm.
Matching does not add conversions; string formatting follows the
[string context rules](strings.md). Traditional `switch`
allows shared empty labels and rejects reachable fallthrough from non-empty branches.
Constant patterns support integers, booleans, strings, and explicitly qualified
enum members. Double literal patterns, destructuring, and guards are not
supported; wildcard and binding arms can handle other selector types.

## Type tests and checked casts

```typescript
func rectangleArea(value: Measurable): int {
  if (value is Rectangle) {
    return value.width * value.height;
  }
  return value.measure();
}

func requireRectangle(value: Measurable): Rectangle {
  return value as Rectangle;
}
```

`is` tests runtime type and narrows stable bindings on the matching branch.
`as` checks the type and reports a runtime cast failure on mismatch. Neither
performs a numeric conversion. Numeric conversions remain explicit
`toInt()`/`toDouble()` operations.

## Class construction from fields

Class members are public by default. Private names start with `#` in declarations and
accesses, such as `#count` and `this.#count`. Visibility modifiers and access sections
are not supported.
When a class has no explicit constructor parameter list, each public instance
field declares a same-name named constructor parameter. No field modifier is needed:

```typescript
class Counter {
  value: int;
  step: int = 1;

  #count: int = 0;

  constructor {
    // Fields corresponding to public parameters are initialized before this body executes.
  }

  next(): int {
    this.value = this.value + this.step;
    this.#count = this.#count + 1;
    return this.value;
  }
}

func main(): void {
  functionDemo();
  genericDemo();
  interfaceDemo();
  enumDemo();

  const counter: Counter = Counter(value: 40);
  print(counter.next());               // 41
}
```

Generated constructor arguments are named: a public instance field without an
initializer is required, and one with an initializer supplies the default when
omitted. Nullable types allow null values but do not make arguments optional:
`text: string?` is required, while `text: string? = null` may be omitted.
Private and static fields do not create constructor parameters. Private fields
need an initializer, a field-formal parameter, or constructor-body assignment; static fields need
an initializer. Calls retain `ClassName(...)` syntax without `new`.

`constructor { ... }` is an optional body for the generated constructor, not
a zero-argument parameter declaration. Fields corresponding to public parameters initialize before that
body runs. Explicit arguments evaluate once in source order. Omitted defaults
then evaluate in field declaration order, followed by the constructor body.
A supplied argument skips its field's default. Defaults cannot access `this`
or caller locals. Each omitted default is evaluated for each construction;
an array default such as `values: int[] = []` creates an independent array for
each instance. Construction keeps its newly allocated receiver rooted. Pure field constructors store
arguments directly into fields; forwarding ordinary parameters to an explicit base
constructor uses a parameter window resolved at compile time.

Classes requiring hand-written parameters can instead declare
`constructor(name: Type, ...) { ... }`. That list defines the complete constructor
signature; fields do not add parameters. `constructor()` therefore declares a
zero-argument constructor. Defaults still run before the body, which must assign
any fields left uninitialized:

```typescript
class Box {
  value: int;
  text: string = '';

  #adjustment: int = 2;

  constructor(initial: int) {
    this.value = initial + this.#adjustment;
  }
}

const box = Box(initial: 40); // value = 42; no value/text constructor arguments
```

Parameter binding and field offsets are resolved at compile time. There is
no runtime annotation execution, reflection, or argument-name dictionary.

For explicit constructors, defaults run before the body; definite initialization
analysis requires every field to be initialized on every returning path. Reading
an uninitialized field, calling an instance method, or exposing `this` before
initialization is rejected. `#name` is available only in the declaring class lexical
scope, including its closures. Base and derived declarations of the same private name
have independent field slots and methods. Public `name` and private `#name` are distinct
members. Private members do not override and cannot be accessed through `super.#name`.
Static private members require the declaring class. Access through a dynamic receiver
inside that scope checks the declaring class at runtime; outside code cannot bypass privacy.

Changing `name` to `#name` deletes the old member and creates a private member. Retained version
handles or closures that still reference the deleted member block an Update until those references
are released or a Reload occurs. With the same private name, class closures keep their lexical
declaring class while accessing the current field.

Vela provides the `#constructor(...)` extension, callable only from its declaring class,
for example through a public static factory. `constructor(this.#value)` binds the private
field to the visible parameter name `value`, so callers write `ClassName(value: ...)`.

An instance `const` field is initialized once during construction. Defaults, field-formal
parameters and body assignments all count as initialization. Branches, loops and exception
paths must establish exactly one initialization on every normal exit. Later assignments,
compound writes and increments are rejected, including dynamic and reflected writes.
This is a shallow binding restriction: array and object contents remain mutable, and the
value need not be a compile-time constant. Static const fields are readonly after lazy initialization.

Inheritance follows four constructor rules. An absent base class or a base with no
parameters contributes an empty parameter list.

| Derived declaration | Constructor parameters | Base call |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No `constructor` | Base parameters followed by own public instance fields | Automatically forward base arguments |
| `constructor { ... }` without `super(...)` | Base parameters followed by own public instance fields | Automatically call the base, then execute the body |
| `constructor { ... super(...); ... }` | Own public instance fields only | Execute the written base call |
| `constructor(...)` | Exactly the explicit parameter list | Execute a written `super(...)`, or forward `super.param` parameters automatically |

The first three forms require named arguments, including when the base declares an
explicit parameter list. Explicit parameter constructors accept positional and named
arguments.
Merged signatures preserve base parameter names, types, requiredness and defaults, then
append own public fields in declaration order. Duplicate parameter names are compile
errors; use an explicit parameter list to resolve the conflict.
Private and static fields contribute no parameters. A private base constructor cannot be
automatically inherited or called.

```typescript
class Component<P> {
  props: P;
}

class ProgressBar extends Component<int> {
  width: int = 100;
  constructor { this.width += 1; }
}

const bar = ProgressBar(props: 42); // props = 42, width = 101
const create: (int, int) => ProgressBar = ProgressBar;
```

Explicit lists support field-binding parameters `this.field` and base-forwarding
parameters `super.param`. Each inherits its target's type, requiredness and default; a
forwarding declaration cannot repeat the type or override the default.
`this.field` binds an own instance field, including a private field. `super.param` names a
parameter in the direct base constructor signature. Neither creates a body-local variable;
read fields through `this.field`.
An ordinary `name: Type` parameter remains a local variable. Matching names do not
implicitly assign fields or forward arguments.

```typescript
class Counter { value: int = 40; }

class BonusCounter extends Counter {
  bonus: int = 2;
  constructor(super.value, this.bonus);
}

const counter = BonusCounter(); // value = 40, bonus = 2
const other = BonusCounter(41, 1);
```

`constructor(...);` is equivalent to the same list with an empty body. A constructor
cannot combine `super.param` with a written `super(...)`.
Without a written base call, forwarding parameters must supply every required base
parameter. Ordinary parameters do not forward automatically.
Compute base arguments with an explicit call:

```typescript
class ComputedCounter extends Counter {
  bonus: int;
  constructor { super(value: this.bonus * 20); }
}

const computed = ComputedCounter(bonus: 2); // value = 40, bonus = 2
```

An automatic base call runs before the derived constructor body. A written `super(...)`
executes at its source position, exactly once on every normal construction path.
Public instance fields must be initialized before entering the base. Private fields may
be assigned afterward when base construction cannot observe them. The analysis follows
virtual dispatch and transitive calls, field reads and writes, receiver escapes and closure
captures. New derived overrides revalidate ancestor initialization proofs. Every instance
field must be initialized before construction returns normally. Field defaults, generated
field parameters and `this.field` bindings take effect before the constructor body.

```typescript
class Panel { const title: string; const closable: bool = true; }
class TitledPanel extends Panel {
  const prefix: string;
  const #fullHeader: string;
  constructor(this.prefix, rawTitle: string, closable: bool = true) {
    super(title: '${this.prefix}: ${rawTitle}', closable: closable);
    this.#fullHeader = '[${this.title}]';
  }
  get header(): string { return this.#fullHeader; }
}
```

Omitted base defaults are evaluated once in the base declaration environment. Omission
remains distinct from explicit null.
These rules apply through generic substitution, multiple inheritance levels, constructor
values, Typed JSON and all execution modes.

## Static members

```typescript
class Counts {

  static #count: int = 0;

  static next(): int {
    Counts.#count = Counts.#count + 1;
    return Counts.#count;
  }
}
```

Static fields require initializers. Each field initializes lazily on first
access and then persists across executions of the same compiled program.
Program copies share this state; separate compilations do not. Initializer
cycles report `CyclicInitialization`; failed initialization resets the active
initializer state for a later attempt. Static slots remain GC roots as long
as the program is alive. Static methods have no `this` and resolve directly.

## Explicit numeric conversions

```typescript
const whole: int = 42.9.toInt();
const fraction: double = whole.toDouble();
```

`int` and `double` expose `toInt()` / `toDouble()`. Double-to-int truncates
toward zero; non-finite values and values outside `[-2^63, 2^63)` report
`InvalidNumericConversion`. Int-to-double rounds according to binary64 and
can lose precision beyond 53 significant bits. Same-type conversions preserve
the value, including signed zero. These operations allocate no GC objects.
Arithmetic, assignment, arguments, and results still forbid implicit numeric
conversion. `is` and `as` do not perform numeric conversion.

`int.parse` / `int.tryParse` and `double.parse` / `double.tryParse` explicitly
convert complete strings to numbers. Integer parsing checks signed int64 bounds;
tryParse returns null for invalid text. See [numeric parsing](numeric_parse.md)
for radix selection, floating-point grammar, and errors.

## Fixed byte storage

`ByteArray(length: int)` owns zero-initialized, fixed-length raw bytes. Indexed
reads return int; writes require int values in 0..255. `ByteArray.from(int[])` and
`slice()` copy storage. `ByteData.view(bytes, ...)` shares and retains the owner
and provides checked unaligned integer/float access with Endian enum arguments.
Neither byte type implicitly converts to int[] or string. See
[byte storage and typed views](byte_data.md).

## Regular expressions

`RegExp` and `RegExpMatch` are built-in reference types with identity equality.
They support nullable annotations, fields, closures, invariant containers and
async payloads. RegExpMatch is created by searches; all properties and match
indexing are read-only. Coordinates count Unicode code points. See
[regular expressions](regexp.md) and the [example](../../examples/regexp.vela).

## Ordered Set and Map

```typescript
const names: Set<string> = Set<string>();
names.add("Vela");                  // bool: true when inserted
names.has("Vela");                  // bool
names.delete("Vela");               // bool: true when removed
names.clear();                       // void
const count: int = names.size;
const items: string[] = names.values();

const scores: Map<string, int> = {'Vela': 42};
scores.set('Dart', 40);              // void
const score: int? = scores.get("Vela");
const keys: string[] = scores.keys();
const values: int[] = scores.values();

for (const key in scores) {
  const value = scores.get(key);
  if (value != null) { print('${key}: ${value}'); }
}
```

An annotated destination also permits `Set()` or `Map()` with contextual type
arguments. Types are invariant; null keys/values require nullable parameters.
`get()` returns null for a missing key; `has()` distinguishes missing entries
from a stored null. Maps also expose `has`, `delete`, `clear`, and `size`.
Snapshot arrays preserve insertion order. Updating an existing key retains its
position; removal and reinsertion place it last. Strings compare by contents,
reference values by identity, all NaNs are the same key, and +0/-0 are the same
key. Ordinary numeric equality keeps its existing IEEE semantics.

Collection loops bind one read-only name. A Map loop iterates a snapshot of its
keys in insertion order; `get(key)` reads the current value and returns null if
the key has been removed. Use `for (const value in scores.values())` to iterate
a value snapshot. Loop bindings do not support destructuring.

Keys and values use typed contiguous storage with an open-addressed hash index
and insertion-order links. Lookup/update is expected amortized O(1); snapshots,
clearing and live-entry tracing are O(size). String-key hashing additionally
costs O(key byte length). Capacity growth and compaction
occasionally cost O(size). Backing allocations count toward heap pressure and
are released by GC. Arrays are growable `T[]`; no duplicate `List<T>` container
is introduced. See [growable arrays](arrays.md).

### Map literals

`{key: value}` creates an ordinary `Map<K, V>`, with trailing commas and nested
arrays or maps. Both sides are expressions: `key` reads a variable, while `'key'`
is a string. A `Map<K, V>` context checks each entry; otherwise key and value
types are inferred independently without merging int/double or heterogeneous
types. Empty `{}` requires a Map context; dynamic alone does not determine its
arguments. Null needs an established nullable or dynamic type; void is invalid.

```vela
const names = {'language': 'Vela'};
const empty: Map<string, int> = {};
const payload: Map<string, dynamic> = {'name': 'Vela', 'age': 7};
const make: (int) => Map<string, int> = value => ({'answer': value});
```

Each evaluation creates a fresh Map, then evaluates each key, checks its
conversion, evaluates its value, checks that conversion, and inserts the entry.
Expressions run once in source order. Duplicate keys replace values while
retaining first insertion order, and still evaluate every expression. Failure
stops later entries and preserves external effects. Reference values are shared
as with `set`; const does not freeze the collection.

A statement beginning with `{` and a lambda's `=> {` always open blocks. Standalone
Map expression statements and Map lambda expression bodies require parentheses.
`=> {}` is an empty block; `() => ({})` returns an empty Map with a Map result
context. Leading `<K, V>{...}`, field shorthand, Set literals, destructuring and
collection spread are unsupported. See the [Map literal design (Chinese)](../zh-CN/destructuring_spread.md)
for execution and tooling contracts.

## Unicode code points and graphemes

```typescript
const text: string = "e\u0301🇨🇳";
const points: int[] = text.codePoints();
const clusters: string[] = text.graphemes();
const count: int = text.graphemeLength;
const first: string = text.graphemeSlice(0, 1);
```

Strings remain validated UTF-8. Existing `length`, indexing, `slice`, and
search offsets use Unicode code points. Grapheme APIs use extended grapheme
clusters, with an inclusive start and exclusive end. Invalid slice bounds
report `IndexOutOfBounds`. No normalization or locale-specific tailoring is
performed. Segmentation uses pinned utf8proc 2.12.0 / Unicode 18.0.0.
`codePoints()` and `graphemes()` materialize exact-sized arrays through linear
passes; they do not rescan a string once per indexed element. Grapheme length
and slicing scan linearly; they do not promise constant-time random access.

## Execution and ownership

Calls, including recursion and closures, use native entries with logical trace
frames and physical-stack protection. Call-depth or stack exhaustion reports
`StackOverflow`; ordinary caught/returned errors allow another call.
Mutable captures use shared GC cells, constant captures use values, and method
values keep their receiver alive. Bound functions and closures currently
allocate GC objects. Class and interface virtual calls share precomputed selector
tables. Selector identities distinguish declaring members and getter/setter kinds;
each receiver type maps them to its implementations. Closed AOT retains implementations
needed by reachable selectors and receivers. A proven unique target or exact receiver
type allows a direct-call optimization without changing polymorphic behavior.

Program metadata is validated at compilation/loading, then shared immutably.
Layout tables are shared across functions. The owning Isolate must outlive
programs, function handles, and their borrowed layouts. Exact roots and write
barriers cover captures, static slots, and collections.
Large-object tracing is not subdivided into per-entry work budgets, so the
incremental collector does not guarantee a hard maximum pause time.

# Source file docs/en/type_inference.md

# Type inference

[**English**](type_inference.md) | [简体中文](../zh-CN/type_inference.md)


Vela checks expressions in two directions: an expression synthesizes its type,
and an enclosing declaration or operation may supply an expected type. This is
compile-time inference; it does not introduce `any`, runtime type discovery, or
numeric conversions. Named functions, methods, and external declarations retain
explicit parameter and return annotations.

## Generic calls and shared constraints

Generic declarations may specify one `extends` bound per parameter. Definitions
in every loaded module are checked before instantiation, using only the capabilities
declared by those bounds. See [generics](generics.md) for declaration and execution contracts.

Generic functions, instance/static methods, class construction, and transparent
generic constructor aliases may omit all type arguments. Arguments, expected
result types, callback signatures, and declaration bounds contribute constraints
before specialization. Explicit arguments fix their parameters; inference cannot
replace them. Type annotations such as `Box<int>` and `Map<string, int>`
must remain complete; later statements do not determine an earlier variable's type.

```typescript
func identity<T>(value: T): T { return value; }
func apply<T, U>(operation: (T) => U, value: T): U { return operation(value); }
class Box<T> { value: T; }

const id = identity(42);
const box = Box(value: id);
const operation: (int) => int = identity;
const answer = apply(value => value + 2, 40);
const scores: Map<string, int> = Map();
```

Ordinary arguments supply evidence before dependent lambdas, generic function
values, and empty constructions are checked. Nested calls also wait when an
output type variable requires context from later arguments. A callback may precede
the argument that supplies its parameter types. Initializers, assignments, fields, constructor
and function arguments, returns, conditionals, `??`, and `await` pass expected
types through the same expression checker. An expected type is an inference hint;
the final assignment relation still has to hold.

Array `map/reduce`, Set/Map/Completer construction, Future factories, and user
generics share the constraint solver. Future adoption and the array result of
`wait` remain intrinsic API semantics. Ordinary callbacks require exact arity,
array callbacks may omit trailing parameters, and exception callbacks filter by
their declared throwable type. These contracts do not create separate inference rules.

Without a relevant declaration bound, inference merges equal types and existing
nullable relationships. Bounds can additionally supply evidence through actual
class inheritance or explicit interface implementation: `T extends Reader<E>` can
infer E as int from T's `Reader<int>` implementation. Parameter dependencies and
F-bounds propagate together and must produce a unique most-specific valid solution.
Inference does not guess arbitrary application supertypes, merge int/double, invent
union types, or change invariant container arguments. Array literals still use
their array context.

Insufficient evidence, conflicting constraints, and incompatible final arguments
are errors. Inference never defaults to dynamic or fills a missing argument with
its bound. `const values = Map()`, context-free `const operation = identity`, and
a context-free `empty()` for a declaration `empty<T extends Reader<int>>(): T[]` cannot obtain missing
arguments this way. Dynamic cannot prove an explicit bound; an unbounded result
can include dynamic only when the source actually has that type.

```vela
interface Reader<E> { read(): E; }
class IntReader implements Reader<int> { read(): int { return 42; } }
func read<T extends Reader<E>, E>(source: T): E { return source.read(); }
func main(): int { return read(IntReader()); }
```

Each generic call owns its inference variables. Solved canonical type arguments
request specialization; explicit and inferred uses share the same concrete
declaration. Inference variables never reach backends. Deferred checks retain
flow facts from their source position and apply possible assignment/call effects
at that position. Runtime evaluation remains exactly once, from left to right.

## Map literal contexts

An expected `Map<K, V>` passes separate contexts into every key and value,
including aliases, nullable containers, nested empty collections, lambdas and
generic function values. Empty `{}` can wait for another generic argument to
supply context: `apply({}, 42)` infers int for `T` in
`apply<T>(values: Map<string, T>, value: T): T`.

Without context, nonempty literals infer keys and values independently, without
merging int/double or defaulting to dynamic. Null does not seed inference.
Both `const m = {}` and `const m: dynamic = {}` report
`empty map requires an expected map type`. Heterogeneous entries require explicit
dynamic key/value types. Container arguments remain invariant; literal contexts
check and convert entries without converting existing containers.

A lambda returning a Map directly uses `value => ({'answer': value})`;
`=> {}` always denotes a block. Map entries and nested expressions share the
constraint solver and flow facts. Checking never changes runtime key/value order.

## Lambda parameters

An expected function type supplies the types of omitted lambda parameters by
position. This applies uniformly to annotated local/global variables, assignments,
returns, class fields and constructor arguments, function arguments, arrays of
callbacks, interfaces, and generic calls after constraint solving.
Aliases and nullable function types carry the same context. Explicit annotations
are still allowed and must satisfy the expected signature.

```typescript
func apply(value: int, operation: (int) => int): int {
  return operation(value);
}

func makeAdder(): (int) => (int) => int {
  return left => right => left + right;
}

func main(): void {
  const add: (int, int) => int = (left, right) => left + right;
  print(apply(21, value => value * 2));

  const values = [3, 1, 2];
  values.sort((left, right) => left - right);
  values.forEach(value => { print(value); });
  print(values.reduce((sum, value) => sum + value, 0));
}
```

A single unannotated parameter may omit parentheses. Multiple parameters and
annotated parameters require parentheses. Parameter counts must match exactly.
Without a function type context, parameter annotations remain necessary:
`const twice = (value: int) => value * 2` is valid, while
`const twice = value => value * 2` reports that `value` needs an annotation or
function type context. The checker does not guess parameter types from operators
or later calls.

## Lambda results

An explicit return annotation takes precedence. Otherwise an expected function
type supplies the result type and checks every return against it. It also
provides context for returned callbacks and empty array literals.

Without a result context, the checker synthesizes the result from expression or
block returns. Equal types merge unchanged; `T` and null merge into `T?`, as do
`T` and `T?`. Different primitive types, including int versus double, do not
merge. Bare returns and value returns cannot mix. No returns means `void`.
A null-only result requires an explicit nullable return annotation. Non-void
blocks must return or throw on every path; inference does not bypass flow checks.
Nested lambda results are collected independently, and closure capture rules
remain unchanged.

## Array callback contexts

Array algorithms supply ordinary function signatures to the same checker; no
special lambda typing rule belongs to `sort` or `some`. `map` supplies its
input parameter type and infers the result array element type from the callback.
For `reduce`, `initialValue` supplies the accumulator type, which can differ
from the element type. Direct lambda bodies are checked with that completed
signature even though the callback precedes `initialValue`. The initial value is
required; omitting it is a compile-time error.
Runtime argument evaluation remains once in source order.

This follows TypeScript's contextual callback inference. TypeScript 6.0.3's
`lib.es5.d.ts` declares a separate accumulator type `U` for
`reduce<U>(callbackfn: (previousValue: U, currentValue: T, ...) => U, initialValue: U): U`.
Strict-mode checks infer number/number parameters for numeric accumulation and
string/number for string accumulation over the same `number[]`. Vela uses
callback-first argument order. Array callbacks may omit unused trailing parameters;
the compiler checks their declared prefix and passes exactly that many arguments.
Ordinary function calls retain their exact arity contract. The remaining intentional
JavaScript differences are documented in [growable arrays](arrays.md).

## Typed IR and editor contracts

The semantic model owns each completed lambda signature. Lowering uses that
signature for parameter registers, return types, captures, and callable layouts.
Source annotations may be absent; backends must not infer or recover types from
AST annotation text. A regression test compares instruction streams and register
counts for equivalent explicit and inferred callbacks.

The language server uses the same checked signature for inferred parameter
hover, completion, and definition lookup. Incomplete expressions retain registered
signatures and established local types; diagnostics do not discard known semantic facts.
Formatting preserves omitted annotations
and supports both parenthesized and single-parameter forms.

## Implementation contracts

Equivalent explicit and inferred callbacks produce equivalent Typed IR and parameter contracts. Inference is performed strictly at compile time; it introduces no runtime dynamic type discovery, boxing, or callback conversion overhead.

# Source file docs/en/generics.md

# Generic bounds and inference

[**English**](generics.md) | [简体中文](../zh-CN/generics.md)

Vela supports generic declarations, one upper bound per parameter, and inference
driven by arguments, context, and bounds. Concrete applications are monomorphized;
primitive values retain their compact storage.

```vela
interface Comparable<T> { compareTo(other: T): int; }
class Score implements Comparable<Score> {
  value: int;
  compareTo(other: Score): int { return this.value - other.value; }
}
func compare<T extends Comparable<T>>(left: T, right: T): int {
  return left.compareTo(right);
}
func main(): int { return compare(Score(value: 42), Score(value: 40)); }
```

The parameter T keeps its identity. Its bound grants capabilities and constrains
applications; it does not replace T with `Comparable<T>`. The complete runnable
example is [examples/generics.vela](../../examples/generics.vela).

## Declarations and bounds

Functions, classes, interfaces, transparent aliases, class instance/static
methods, and interface methods can declare `<T, U extends T>` parameters.
Constructors use their class parameters and cannot declare another parameter list.
All names in a list are registered before bounds are resolved, so a bound can
reference a later parameter. Duplicate names in one list are errors. A method
parameter can shadow an owner parameter; identity includes the declaration and
parameter index.

Type annotations require complete applications such as `Box<int>`. Calls and
ordinary function contexts may omit the entire argument list. Explicit lists
must be complete; there are no raw types, partial lists, or default arguments.

A bound may use existing primitive, enum, class, interface, array, function, or
parameterized value types, their nullable forms, and parameters in scope.
Qualified names and transparent aliases use normal module/type resolution.
`void`, the null-literal type, and dynamic are invalid explicit bounds. Omitting
a bound leaves a distinct abstract parameter; it does not make it dynamic.

An unbounded parameter may receive nullable types or explicitly supplied dynamic.
Existing return-only uses of void remain valid, while fields, parameters, array
elements, and bounded value positions still reject void. Non-null bounds reject
nullable arguments. Nullable bounds allow appropriate non-null and nullable
arguments, but member access still requires the usual non-null proof. Applying
`T?` to an already nullable argument does not add another nullable wrapper.

Recursive bounds such as `T extends Comparable<T>` are valid. Parameter dependencies
may also be mutually recursive through real type constructors. Forwarding cycles
without a constructor, such as `T extends T` or `T extends U, U extends T`, are
errors, including cycles hidden by transparent aliases. Real type nesting and
generic expansion are each limited to 128 levels.

## Static checking

Every generic definition in every loaded module is checked before instantiation,
including unused functions, classes, interfaces, and aliases. Bounds determine
available members and static relations. Locals, fields, closures, returns, async,
and flow analysis use the normal checker. A concrete application cannot supply
capabilities missing from the declaration.

Unbounded T can be passed, captured, stored in legal parameterized types, and
returned. Operations need a suitable bound or an ordinary function argument.
An upper bound does not grant construction capability: use `() => T` rather
than `T()` when a factory is needed. A bound value cannot be returned as an
arbitrary caller-selected T.

Static proof uses type identity, nullability, class inheritance, and explicit
interface implementations. Nominal identity includes the defining module,
declaration, and canonical arguments. Equal member names do not establish an
interface implementation. The same nominal relation governs argument binding
and bounds. Checked dynamic conversion remains a separate operation; dynamic
cannot prove a bound. Use `is` or `as` to establish a concrete type first.

User generic applications and mutable arrays, Set, and Map remain invariant.
Future retains its existing payload-adoption contract without creating general
generic covariance. There is no int/double promotion or implicit common numeric
supertype. Function assignment and overrides retain their existing signature
rules; no general function subtyping is introduced.

Aliases validate their own bounds and every application in their expanded target.
For example, an unconstrained alias cannot forward T to a declaration requiring
`T extends Reader<int>`. Aliases do not create runtime nominal types.

## Inference and function values

Explicit arguments fix their parameters. Otherwise argument types, expected
results, callbacks, and declaration bounds enter one constraint domain. Parameter
dependencies, invariant equalities, nominal projections, and recursive bounds
propagate together until a unique most-specific valid solution is available.

```vela
interface Reader<E> { read(): E; }
class IntReader implements Reader<int> { read(): int { return 42; } }
func read<T extends Reader<E>, E>(source: T): E { return source.read(); }
func main(): int { return read(IntReader()); }
```

Here E is inferred from the actual `Reader<int>` implementation. Conflicting
nominal paths are errors. For an F-bound `X extends A<X>`, an argument of class C
can select B through the explicit chain `C extends B`, `B extends A<B>`; solving
is not limited to trying C and checking its bound afterward. Without a relevant
bound, ordinary inference retains strict equal-type and nullable merging.

No evidence means no default. A context-free call to
`func empty<T extends Reader<int>>(): T[]` cannot select its bound as T. Inconsistent
or incomparable valid candidates produce diagnostics. Inference never selects
dynamic, an arbitrary parent, or the first implementation path to hide ambiguity.

Dependent lambdas, generic function/method values, empty constructions, and
nested calls wait for sufficient context, including through conditional, match,
coalescing, and array expressions. Deferred checking retains source-position flow
facts and effects. Runtime evaluation remains exactly once in source order.

An ordinary function type can specialize a generic value:

```vela
func identity<T>(value: T): T { return value; }
func main(): int {
  const operation: (int) => int = identity;
  return operation(42);
}
```

Without sufficient context, an open generic value is an error. There are no
runtime polymorphic function values or generic lambdas. Array callbacks retain
their existing prefix-parameter contract; ordinary callbacks require exact arity.

## Methods, interfaces, and execution

Receiver arguments determine owner parameters before method parameters are solved.
Static methods follow the existing owner binding rules. Captured method values
retain their receiver and concrete application using the ordinary closure layout.
Interface selectors carry concrete method arguments and every reachable explicit
implementation. Generic implementations and overrides must match parameter counts,
normalized bounds, and method signatures after alpha renaming. They cannot tighten
a caller's contract.

Dynamic receivers cannot supply an open method declaration. Narrow or cast to a
known class/interface before a generic method call. Ordinary non-generic dynamic
calls retain their existing checked boundary.

The frontend publishes separate abstract-definition facts and concrete execution
facts, including parameter identity, canonical applications, final signatures,
and resolved targets. Backends consume concrete types and targets without solving
inference variables or interpreting generated names. Bounds require no runtime generic solver. GC, exceptions, async, interface dispatch, JIT, and AOT use existing
concrete runtime contracts.

Host imports and AOT exports retain concrete signatures. Script generics can call
concrete C++ bindings; they cannot expose an open generic host ABI. Standalone
native distribution includes required concrete implementations before publication.

## Persistence and tools

Declaration contracts retain normalized bounds and nominal references. Cache and
native-image identity cover these facts. Parameter counts, semantic bounds, or
interface method-contract changes require Reload. Alpha renames, equivalent
transparent bounds, and import-prefix changes preserve semantic identity.
Reload creates a fresh Isolate. Implementation-body updates preserve the ordinary
version protocol: old frames, closures, suspended continuations, and deoptimization
records keep their own concrete signatures.

Unused definitions support parameter/bound hover, definition lookup, and bound-member
completion. Type-parameter rename respects lexical identity and bound references,
and rejects capture or collision. Formatting, documentation, semantic tokens,
editor highlighting, and persistent REPL use the same syntax and type contracts.
Incomplete trailing input does not discard facts from retained complete declarations.

See [type inference](type_inference.md), [core language](core_language.md),
[modules](modules.md), and [source tools](source_tooling.md). The
[Chinese specification](../zh-CN/generics.md#8-诊断与验证矩阵) also records the compiler
validation matrix and implementation acceptance boundaries.

# Source file docs/en/modules.md

# Modules

[**English**](modules.md) | [简体中文](../zh-CN/modules.md)


Every source file has a separate top-level scope. Functions, classes, enums,
interfaces, aliases, and module-level `let`/`const` bindings are private to that
file unless marked `export`. Class members are public by default, with `#name`
restricting access to the declaring class lexical scope, independently of whether the class is exported.

```typescript
// counters.vela
let current: int = 40;
export const step: int = 1;
export func next(): int {
  current = current + step;
  return current;
}
```

```typescript
// main.vela
import 'counters' as counter;
func main(): int {
  counter.next();
  return counter.next();
}
```

An import without `as` brings the dependency's exports into the importing
module's top-level scope. An import with `as` requires qualified access, such
as `counter.next()`. Classes, enum types, generic applications, and type aliases
also support qualification. Conflicting imports or top-level declarations
produce diagnostics; use prefixes to distinguish imports. Local variables and
parameters can shadow imported names or prefixes.

Imports are not implicit re-exports. A dependency cannot use the entry module's
private symbols, and importing a module does not expose its own dependencies.
Import prefixes are compile-time bindings, not runtime objects or values.
There is no `namespace` declaration block.

Files are loaded once by canonical path using a work queue. Cyclic imports can
link function declarations without recursively evaluating module bodies. Module
bindings and type names are resolved before generic specialization; calls and
field offsets use resolved native targets and layout metadata without module-name lookup at runtime.

Module globals reuse the program's rooted lazy initializer slots. They initialize
on demand and persist across executions and copies of the same program. A new
compilation gets separate state. A mutable exported `let` can be assigned through
an import, while assigning to a `const` is a compile error. Const prevents rebinding,
not mutation of the referenced object. Initializers use the defining module's
scope and cannot capture the local variables of a caller or another initializer's
lambda. Inference follows global dependencies; cyclic inference requires explicit
types, and a cycle during actual lazy initialization reports `CyclicInitialization`.

`CompileModules` and `CheckModules` accept named `SourceInput` entries and an
entry path. Relative imports resolve only among the supplied inputs. They do
not silently read the disk. `CheckFile` accepts content overlays for unsaved
editor buffers while retaining the file-backed dependency graph.

Use source files as compiler entry points. Import paths resolve relative to the
importing file. An extensionless specifier such as `import 'math';` resolves
directly to `math.vela`; an explicit extension remains valid. Resolution does not
probe an extensionless file or an `index.vela` directory entry. The loader,
compilation cache, editor navigation and import links share the same resolution.
Standard objects such as `Math` and `Error` are available without
imports; `std:` imports are no longer supported.

`import 'sdk:test';` loads the testing library from immutable source embedded in
the distribution. SDK modules follow ordinary export, privacy and prefix rules.
File and memory compilation, native object caches and language services share the
`sdk:test` identity; memory inputs cannot override it. Unknown `sdk:` modules
are errors and are never resolved as files. `builtin:` remains an internal
standard-environment identity. See the [testing contract](../zh-CN/testing.md).

# Source file docs/en/exceptions.md

# Exceptions

[**English**](exceptions.md) | [简体中文](../zh-CN/exceptions.md)


`throw` accepts a non-null class or interface value. Catch clauses test concrete
class identity or explicit interface implementation in source order. Values and
numbers are never converted to error objects implicitly.

```typescript
class ValidationError {
  message: string;
}

func validate(value: int): int {
  if (value < 0) { throw ValidationError(message: "negative value"); }
  return value;
}

func main(): int {
  try {
    return validate(-1);
  } catch (error: ValidationError) {
    print(error.message);
    return 42;
  } catch (error: Error) {
    print(error.message);
    return 1;
  } finally {
    print("finished");
  }
}
```

A final `catch { ... }` handles any exception without exposing an untyped value.
Typed bindings require `catch (name: Type)`. Duplicate types and catch clauses
after a catch-all are rejected. A try must have catch, finally, or both. Catch
bindings follow ordinary lexical scope and mutable closure-capture rules.

`catch (error: dynamic)` also catches every exception and binds its original
instance for generic exception handling and matching. It must be the final
catch clause. Access through the binding follows the normal dynamic checks.

The default global `Error(message: string, code: string)` requires no import;
`code` defaults to `"Error"`. This is an ordinary fixed-layout class. Runtime failures
are materialized as this type: `message` contains the diagnostic, while `code`
contains the stable `ExecutionStatusCode`, for example `"DivisionByZero"` or
`"NativeFailure"`. Diagnostic wording is separate and may change without changing
the code. Domain APIs document their own named codes. An explicitly constructed
Error retains its supplied code unchanged. Custom error types require no inheritance or common
base class. Native failures and runtime checked operations use the same catch path.

[Numeric parsing](numeric_parse.md) defines `IntParseError`, `DoubleParseError`,
and `InvalidRadix`; [UTC conversion](time.md) defines `DateParseError` and
`DateRangeError`. These use the same Error/catch mechanism. tryParse turns only
invalid numeric text or int64 overflow into null; invalid radix still throws.

Async completion errors use `FutureAlreadyCompleted` for a second completion request
and `FutureSelfAdoption` for a direct or indirect adoption cycle. `TimeoutException`
is an independent throwable class whose default code is `Timeout`. An external
`Future<T>` completing with an incompatible value or a non-throwable error produces
`TypeError`. `AsyncIdle` is an embedding/test execution status when a Future has no
producer that can advance it; it is not an exception injected into the pending task.
The standalone program driver keeps waiting for its root and does not treat idle
as failure.
See [async contracts](async_tasks.md) for propagation and scheduling.

Finally executes on normal completion, return, break, continue, and exception
propagation. Return expressions are evaluated once before finally; changing a
local in finally cannot replace the previously computed return value. A return,
break, continue, or throw inside finally replaces the pending completion. Errors
inside a finally block are handled by outer regions, never by that same try's
catch clauses. Only finalizers exited by a break/continue run; leaving a loop
inside a try does not prematurely exit the try. Finally resolves names in its
own lexical scope, regardless of shadowing inside the protected body.

Compiler checks conservatively discard non-null refinements on catch entry,
because any preceding operation may have modified captured or local state.
Constructor analysis runs finalizers before checking return initialization and
before propagating break/continue initialization states. A catch/finally
exceptional entry cannot assume fields written only inside the try body.

Unhandled results retain the original runtime status, or `Thrown` for explicit
script throws, plus owned source-aware traces. Automatic propagation through
finally preserves the original throwing frames, even when finally calls other
functions or handles another error. An explicit `throw value` starts a new throw
site. A failed lazy initializer resets only the frames actually unwound, so a
caller that catches the error can retry initialization.

## Representation and performance

IR instructions record their innermost handler, and CFG construction includes
exceptional successors before liveness and optimization. Native lowering generates
failure edges to the corresponding catch/finally blocks while retaining source
positions. No C++ exception or nonlocal jump crosses the host boundary.

A hidden GC envelope roots the thrown instance and owns its status and message.
Its separately owned diagnostic retains resolved source-version frames rather
than borrowing code. Catch exposes the typed payload. Pending envelopes remain
precise roots while finally executes; replacing a pending completion makes the old
envelope collectible, including its diagnostic. Heap counters account for the
envelope and inline message, not every host-side diagnostic allocation.
Allocation exhaustion can prevent an error envelope from being created; the
failure is then returned directly as OutOfMemory.

# Source file docs/en/async_tasks.md

# Async Functions and Future Semantics

[**English**](async_tasks.md) | [简体中文](../zh-CN/async_tasks.md)

> Status: implemented. This document defines the async/Future language, runtime, host, and CLI contracts.

## Goals

Vela keeps the familiar `async` / `await` syntax and uses `Future<T>` for asynchronous results. It provides Future-style composition APIs without claiming to match every detail of JavaScript `Promise` or Dart `Future`. A Future is a strongly typed value that can be observed more than once and completes once; failures use Vela's exception contract.

The design covers async functions, Future composition, error propagation, async main, host async operations, cancellation signaling, timers, GC lifetime, and performance validation. Async/await is single-threaded cooperative execution; it does not create parallel work by itself.

## API Example

```vela
class User { name: string; }

external func fetchUser(id: int): Future<User>;

async func loadUsers(ids: int[]): Future<User[]> {
    let first = fetchUser(ids[0]);
    let second = fetchUser(ids[1]);
    return await Future.wait([first, second]);
}

async func main(): Future<int> {
    try {
        let users = await loadUsers([7, 8]);
        print(users[0].name);
        return 0;
    } catch {
        print("Could not load users");
        return 1;
    }
}
```

## Syntax and Types

- Async functions, methods, and closures use the `async` modifier. Their explicit return type is `Future<T>`, and a call expression also has type `Future<T>`.
- An async body may return a `T` or another `Future<T>`; the outer Future adopts that Future's result. An ordinary function may also explicitly return `Future<T>`.
- Function values express their actual call result, for example `(int) => Future<User>`. `async` does not change the function value type, so async functions and ordinary functions returning the same Future type share the same callable contract.
- `await e` is valid only inside an async function. If `e` is `Future<T>`, the result is `T`; for a plain value, the result type is unchanged. Awaiting a nullable Future that is null produces null.
- Async lambdas, instance methods, static methods, and interface implementations follow the same rules. Constructors, static initializers, and module initializers cannot be async; module top level does not allow await.
- `Future<T>` is a built-in generic reference type that can be stored, passed, returned, and captured. A Future adopts only another Vela Future; it does not inspect an arbitrary object's `then` member.

## Future API

```vela
const producer = Completer<int>();
const result = producer.future.then((value) => value + 2);
Timer.after(0, (): void => { producer.complete(40); });
const answer: int = await result;
```

The example runs inside an async function. `Completer<T>()` also accepts a contextual `Completer<T>` type. Its read-only properties are `future: Future<T>` and `isCompleted: bool`. `isCompleted` becomes true when completion is requested, including adoption of a pending Future. `complete(value)` accepts `T` or `Future<T>`; `Completer<void>.complete()` takes no argument. `completeError(error)` requires a non-null class or interface instance. Duplicate completion throws `Error` with code `FutureAlreadyCompleted`; direct or indirect self-adoption throws code `FutureSelfAdoption`.

`then` infers its result from the callback's return type. For a `Future<void>` source, the success callback takes no value parameter. Error callbacks take exactly one non-null class or interface parameter; an unannotated lambda parameter defaults to `Error`. The callback handles matching payload types, and other errors propagate unchanged. `catchError` must return the source value type or a Future of that type. `whenComplete` accepts a zero-argument action returning `void` or `Future<void>`; an asynchronous action finishes before the result is forwarded. Optional callbacks may be null. Erased receivers use the same scheduler and validate retained callback signatures before registering continuations. Callback results that enter a concrete Future payload are checked before completion; see [dynamic values](json.md).

`Future<T>` is covariant in its result type; `Completer<T>` remains invariant.
