# Source file docs/en/regexp.md

# Regular expressions

[**English**](regexp.md) | [简体中文](../zh-CN/regexp.md)

> Status: implemented. RegExp and RegExpMatch use pinned PCRE2 10.49 with Unicode 17.0.0 tables, code-point coordinates and accounted native storage.

Vela uses Dart-style `RegExp` objects and match results, backed by the standalone
PCRE2 library. Patterns follow the pinned PCRE2 version's syntax and matching
rules with the configuration below. Positions use Vela's existing Unicode code
point indices. A pattern is compiled at construction; matching does not mutate
a cursor on the RegExp object. The API makes no ECMAScript compatibility promise.

```vela
func main(): void {
  const pattern = RegExp('([A-Za-z]+)=([0-9]+)');
  const found: RegExpMatch? = pattern.firstMatch('age=42');
  if (found != null) {
    print(found.group(1) ?? ''); // age
    print(found.group(2) ?? ''); // 42
  }

  const numbers = RegExp('[0-9]+');
  const matches: RegExpMatch[] = numbers.allMatches('7, 42');
  print(matches.length); // 2
}
```

This API is independent of dynamic typing and JSON. The first version does not
add a general Pattern/Iterable protocol, regular-expression literals, raw string
syntax, replacement/split APIs, or user callbacks during matching.
[String case conversion](string_case.md) is specified separately.

## RegExp API

| API | Result / contract |
| --- | --- |
| `RegExp(source: string, multiLine?: bool, caseSensitive?: bool, dotAll?: bool)` | Construct and compile a pattern; defaults are false, true, false respectively |
| `RegExp.escape(text: string): string` | Produce a PCRE2 literal pattern fragment for text; output spelling is unspecified |
| `pattern.pattern: string` | Read-only original decoded source string |
| `pattern.isMultiLine: bool` | Read-only multiLine setting |
| `pattern.isCaseSensitive: bool` | Read-only caseSensitive setting |
| `pattern.isDotAll: bool` | Read-only dotAll setting |
| `pattern.isUnicode: bool` | Read-only true; matching always uses Unicode mode |
| `pattern.hasMatch(input: string): bool` | Whether any match exists |
| `pattern.firstMatch(input: string): RegExpMatch?` | First match, or null |
| `pattern.allMatches(input: string, start?: int): RegExpMatch[]` | All non-overlapping matches from start, default zero |
| `pattern.matchAsPrefix(input: string, start?: int): RegExpMatch?` | Anchored matching attempt at start, default zero; return a match or null |
| `pattern.stringMatch(input: string): string?` | The first whole matched substring, or null |

RegExp and RegExpMatch are dedicated built-in reference types, not user
subclasses or dynamic property maps. They support ordinary fields, parameters,
returns, nullable annotations, captures, and invariant typed containers.
RegExpMatch cannot be directly constructed by user code. All properties are
read-only. Register the standard declarations and dependency closure using the
existing reserved-name, local-shadowing, overlay, and cache-fingerprint rules.

Arguments follow ordinary Vela evaluation order and positional/named calling
rules. Optional parameters are omitted arguments, not nullable values. No
implicit number/string conversion is performed.

## Matching and Unicode

PCRE2 defines pattern semantics, including ordered alternatives, greedy/lazy and
possessive quantifiers, captures, backreferences, lookarounds, Unicode property
escapes, and inline options. Matching uses `pcre2_match`, not the DFA interface;
the native backtracking result is exposed. Do not translate patterns into a
different dialect or maintain an ECMAScript grammar checker. PCRE2's own
constraints apply: for example, variable-length lookbehind must have a bounded
maximum length allowed by the pinned build; unlimited repetition in lookbehind
is not promised. Unsupported patterns produce a compile error.

| Setting | Vela contract |
| --- | --- |
| Code unit width | Only the 8-bit library, matching UTF-8 directly |
| `PCRE2_UTF` | Always enabled |
| `PCRE2_UCP` | Always enabled; shorthand classes such as `\d`, `\w`, `\s` use PCRE2 Unicode-property defaults |
| `PCRE2_NEVER_BACKSLASH_C` | Always enabled; `\C` cannot split a UTF-8 character |
| `multiLine` | Maps to `PCRE2_MULTILINE`, initially false |
| `caseSensitive` | False enables `PCRE2_CASELESS`, initially true |
| `dotAll` | Maps to `PCRE2_DOTALL`, initially false |
| Newline convention | Explicit `PCRE2_NEWLINE_ANY` |
| `\R` convention | Explicit `PCRE2_BSR_UNICODE` |
| JIT | Disabled; use the interpreter |

Constructor properties report the initial option values. PCRE2 inline options
and supported pattern directives retain their native meaning, including scoped
overrides. UTF mode and the prohibition on `\C` cannot be relaxed. Leave
ECMAScript-compatibility, locale-specific casing, and allowing `\K` inside
lookarounds disabled; in particular, do not enable
`PCRE2_EXTRA_ALLOW_LOOKAROUND_BSK`, which can produce reversed whole-match spans.
Use the library's default character tables, not tables made from host locale.

Ignore-case matching follows PCRE2's Unicode caseless rules, not full string
case expansion. Do not lowercase or uppercase the subject before matching:
that changes positions and is not the engine's comparison algorithm.

`RegExp.escape` escapes PCRE2 metacharacters and handles literal whitespace and
`#` safely even when its fragment is embedded in extended mode. Scalar hex
escapes may be used where necessary. It does not escape Vela source literals;
the exact generated fragment is not a serialization contract.

Vela strings are valid UTF-8, and all exposed positions count Unicode scalar
values. Unicode mode is mandatory; there is no `unicode: false` option.
`allMatches` eagerly returns the existing `RegExpMatch[]` type rather than adding
a lazy Iterable. Pattern text uses ordinary Vela strings: write
`RegExp('\\d+')` to pass a backslash followed by d to the pattern compiler.
There is no Dart raw-string or JavaScript regex-literal syntax in this version.

Matching preserves the input exactly: there is no normalization, grapheme
segmentation, or locale-dependent behavior. `.` consumes one code point in its
ordinary single-character use, including a supplementary character. Embedded
NUL is supported in both input and pattern; APIs always pass explicit lengths.
Composed and decomposed strings remain distinct unless the pattern matches them
explicitly. Unicode tables are pinned dependency data, never host locale data.

## Positions and repeated matching

For input length N, start must satisfy `0 <= start <= N`; invalid starts use the
existing bounds error. Positions are relative to the original input, and every
match spans the half-open interval `[start, end)`. A start argument controls the
search position, not the input's origin or the context available to anchors and
lookbehind. The engine receives the whole input and a byte start offset.
matchAsPrefix uses `PCRE2_ANCHORED` for that matching attempt. Native `\K` may
reset the reported whole-match start after the anchored attempt began; capture
groups may also span text outside the reported whole match. These are PCRE2
semantics, not an error or a reason to discard a successful result.

```vela
const found = RegExp('Vela').firstMatch('😀Vela');
if (found != null) {
  print(found.start); // 1
  print(found.end);   // 5
}
```

`allMatches` searches from the requested position, then continues from the end
of each nonempty match. After an empty match, advance by one complete code point.
An empty match at N is included once and terminates enumeration. An empty
pattern therefore yields N + 1 empty matches. This rule also applies to empty
matches produced by alternatives or quantifiers.

Calls do not share iteration state. Repeating firstMatch or hasMatch with the
same object and input produces the same result. There is no lastIndex, global,
or sticky flag; matchAsPrefix provides an explicitly anchored operation.

## RegExpMatch API

| API | Result / contract |
| --- | --- |
| `match.start: int` | Whole-match start in code points |
| `match.end: int` | Whole-match exclusive end in code points |
| `match.input: string` | Original input string |
| `match.pattern: RegExp` | RegExp that produced this match |
| `match.groupCount: int` | Capturing-group count, excluding group zero |
| `match.groupNames: string[]` | Snapshot of unique names in PCRE2 name-table order (lexicographic UTF-8 order) |
| `match.group(index: int): string?` | Whole match at zero, capture at 1..groupCount; null if the capture did not participate |
| `match[index]: string?` | Same behavior as group(index); read-only |
| `match.groups(indices: int[]): string?[]` | Requested captures in request order |
| `match.namedGroup(name: string): string?` | Named capture, or null when that defined group did not participate |

An existing capture matching zero characters returns an empty string, not null.
Group zero always participates. Native branch-reset numbering is preserved;
groupCount is the highest valid capture number. If a pattern enables duplicate
names, namedGroup uses PCRE2's selection of the first participating occurrence
and returns null if none participated. An out-of-range numeric group index
throws the existing bounds error; an unknown group name throws `Error` with code
`RegExpGroupError`. Negative indices are not supported. `groups` validates
indices before publishing a result and returns an independent array. Repeated
groupNames access returns independent snapshots; changing a snapshot does not
change compiled metadata.

## Engine, ownership, and failures

Integrate PCRE2 through DEPS and GN with Unicode enabled, only its 8-bit source
closure, and JIT disabled. Its C API returns explicit errors and fits Vela's
exception-free C++ build. Pin an immutable revision and record the actual
BSD-3-Clause WITH PCRE2-exception and bundled data licenses, Unicode table version,
source closure, and build configuration in dependency records. Do not modify
upstream sources or retain another engine as a fallback.

Use a general context with Vela's allocator, a compile context with the settings
above, and operation-owned match data. Matching uses the immutable default
context; mutable work buffers use the accounted pattern allocator. Keep the pinned build's match,
depth, and heap limits explicit in GN configuration and dependency records;
they are implementation limits, and changes require regression review. Translate
`PCRE2_ERROR_MATCHLIMIT`, `PCRE2_ERROR_DEPTHLIMIT`, and `PCRE2_ERROR_HEAPLIMIT`
to a distinct limit error. They are not no-match or physical allocation failure.
Do not set unlimited budgets. These engine counters are not a wall-clock timeout.

PCRE2 receives the original UTF-8 buffer and explicit length and returns byte
offsets. There is no UTF-16 subject copy. Convert public code point starts to
byte starts and capture spans back to code point positions using one shared
boundary mapping per operation. Build it once for allMatches rather than
rescanning prefixes for every capture. The already validated internal UTF-8
contract permits `PCRE2_NO_UTF_CHECK` on repeated matching calls; it never
permits malformed external input or starts inside a code point. Check all size
and index conversions before allocation, without truncating `PCRE2_SIZE` values.
Map compile diagnostics' byte offsets back to decoded-pattern code point offsets.

RegExp owns the compiled program, original pattern, flags, and capture-name
metadata. RegExpMatch strongly retains its input and RegExp and owns immutable
capture spans. No result points into operation-owned match data, work buffers,
or borrowed arena memory. Retain byte spans as well as public coordinate
information so group extraction copies the selected UTF-8 content without
rescanning the whole prefix. A match can outlive both caller variables.

GC traces the input/pattern references and uses existing publication barriers.
Compiled programs and engine work buffers participate in heap memory accounting;
their owner releases them exactly once on failure, collection, or Isolate
destruction. Root receivers, inputs, partial result arrays, and new match objects
before allocation safepoints. hasMatch need not allocate a RegExpMatch; group
extraction allocates a string only when content is requested and cannot be reused.

| Failure | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Invalid pattern syntax or unsupported pattern constraints | `Error` with code `RegExpSyntaxError`, the PCRE2 diagnostic, and a decoded-pattern code point offset |
| Invalid search start or numeric group index | Existing `IndexOutOfBounds` path |
| Unknown named group | `Error` with code `RegExpGroupError` |
| Engine/backing allocation or representable-size exhaustion | Existing recoverable `OutOfMemory` path |
| Match-work, matching-depth, or engine-heap limit reached | `Error` with code `RegExpLimitError` |
| Other engine execution failure | Explicit `RegExpExecutionError`, not a no-match result |
| Wrong static receiver, argument, or index type | Compile-time diagnostic; dynamic native boundaries retain runtime checks |

No match is a normal false, null, or empty-array result. Engine failure is never
reported as no match, and allMatches never returns a partial array. Errors flow
through ordinary catch/finally and source traces; JSON/native failure labels
must not replace regex-specific diagnostics. A caller may reuse the native instance and
RegExp after a caught operation failure.

This is a backtracking engine and has no general linear worst-case guarantee.
The first version exposes no timeout parameter. Allocation, configured limits,
and engine failures remain explicit; performance validation includes ambiguous
quantifiers and failed searches, not just successful literal matches.

## Implementation and validation

The shared [signature registry](../../compiler/frontend/builtins/regexp_builtins.cc)
provides static checking and tooling metadata. [Runtime operations](../../runtime/regexp/regexp.cc)
own compilation, search and captures; [heap integration](../../runtime/heap/heap_regexp.cc)
owns native accounting, tracing and release. Runtime does not depend on the
compiler or tooling. Ordinary string search retains its existing semantics.

The pinned interpreter uses match limit 1,000,000, depth limit 1,000 and heap
limit 8,192 KiB. Parentheses nesting is limited to 250 and maximum variable
lookbehind to 255. Unicode 17.0.0 tables are independent of string casing Unicode
18.0.0 data. [Dependency records](../../third_party/README.md) define the source
closure, licenses and configuration. Image version 7 retains typed layout
operands; native compiled programs are recreated during execution.

[Compiler/image tests](../../compiler/language/regexp_unittest.cc) cover both types,
options, Unicode coordinates, captures, native PCRE2 constructs, method values,
containers, async payloads and errors. [Runtime tests](../../runtime/regexp/regexp_unittest.cc)
check all three resource limits, execution failures, partial-result cleanup,
match-only reachability, native accounting and hasMatch zero GC allocations.
REPL and LSP tests cover persistent ownership, completion, hover and named
arguments. The runnable [example](../../examples/regexp.vela) uses ordinary Vela
string escapes and typed results.

Release benchmarks separate pattern compilation, repeated hasMatch/firstMatch,
allMatches materialization and coordinate mapping, capture extraction, GC
pressure and backtracking limits. Aggregate results, variation and native
workload comparisons are retained in the [rolling summary](../../benchmarks/results/rolling_summary.json).

## References

- [Dart RegExp](https://api.dart.dev/dart-core/RegExp-class.html) and [RegExpMatch](https://api.dart.dev/dart-core/RegExpMatch-class.html).
- [PCRE2 API](https://www.pcre.org/current/doc/html/pcre2api.html) and [pattern syntax](https://www.pcre.org/current/doc/html/pcre2pattern.html); implementation fixtures use the pinned version.
- [PCRE2 source](https://github.com/PCRE2Project/pcre2) and [license](https://github.com/PCRE2Project/pcre2/blob/main/LICENCE.md).
- Vela [strings](strings.md), [exceptions](exceptions.md), and [garbage collection](garbage_collection.md).

# Source file docs/en/time.md

# UTC date and time API

[**English**](time.md) | [简体中文](../zh-CN/time.md)

Vela represents instants as signed int Unix timestamps in milliseconds. The
Date static class provides four conversion methods; DateParts is a
read-only UTC calendar snapshot. Calendar conversion reuses the Abseil Time
implementation already included in the repository's build source list.

```vela
func main(): void {
  const timestamp: int = Date.parse('2026-10-26T12:30:45.123+08:00');
  print(Date.toISOString(timestamp)); // 2026-10-26T04:30:45.123Z

  const parts: DateParts = Date.toUTC(timestamp);
  const restored: int = Date.fromUTC(
    year: parts.year,
    month: parts.month,
    day: parts.day,
    hour: parts.hour,
    minute: parts.minute,
    second: parts.second,
    millisecond: parts.millisecond,
  );
  print(restored == timestamp); // true
}
```

The first version covers UTC calendar conversion and a strict, common ISO 8601 /
RFC 3339 date-time subset with explicit numeric offsets. It adds no DateTime or
Duration type, system-local conversion, named time zone, daylight-saving rules,
locale formatting, arbitrary format strings, or calendar arithmetic. Timers and
scheduling belong to the separate [async contract](async_tasks.md). The API is
independent of dynamic, JSON, and regular expressions.

## Public API

| API | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| `Date.now(): int` | Existing wall-clock Unix timestamp in milliseconds |
| `performance.now(): double` | Existing monotonic reading in milliseconds; subtract readings to measure elapsed time |
| `Date.parse(source: string): int` | Parse the supported explicit-offset date-time format and return Unix milliseconds |
| `Date.toISOString(timestamp: int): string` | Format a supported timestamp as canonical UTC text |
| `Date.fromUTC(year: int, month: int, day: int, hour?: int, minute?: int, second?: int, millisecond?: int): int` | Construct Unix milliseconds from validated UTC fields; omitted time fields are zero |
| `Date.toUTC(timestamp: int): DateParts` | Return a new read-only UTC calendar snapshot |

Date remains a non-constructible standard static class. Date and DateParts need
no import and follow existing reserved-name and local-shadowing rules. The
standard environment must include DateParts when Date declarations refer to it,
even if user code never writes the DateParts name. Internal standard sources
participate in overlay protection and compilation-cache fingerprints.

Optional parameters mean omission, not null. Calls retain ordinary source-order
evaluation and positional/named argument checking, including named time fields
with preceding optional fields omitted. No argument is inferred from the current
date, host time zone, or an earlier call. All numeric parameters and fields are
int; int/double conversion remains explicit.

The clock contracts are unchanged: wall-clock adjustments may move Date.now
forward or backward, while performance.now has an unspecified origin and is
for measuring elapsed time. Equal consecutive readings are valid. A monotonic
reading is not a Unix timestamp and is not an input to the calendar API.

## Calendar, precision, and supported range

Use the proleptic Gregorian calendar, years 1 through 9999, with one-based months
and days. Year 99 means 0099, not 1999. Gregorian leap-year rules apply across
the entire supported range. Each Unix day has 86,400 seconds; leap seconds are
not represented.

| Field | Valid range |
| --- | --- |
| `year` | 1..9999 |
| `month` | 1..12 |
| `day` | 1..the actual number of days in that year/month |
| `hour` | 0..23 |
| `minute` | 0..59 |
| `second` | 0..59 |
| `millisecond` | 0..999 |

No field is normalized into another: month 13, February 30, hour 24, second 60,
negative components, and millisecond 1000 are errors. Validate before narrowing
int arguments to backend field types. Abseil civil-time normalization must not
silently change an invalid requested date.

The four conversion methods support the inclusive timestamp range
`[-62135596800000, 253402300799999]`, corresponding to
`0001-01-01T00:00:00.000Z` through `9999-12-31T23:59:59.999Z`. The normalized UTC
instant must be in range, including after applying an input offset. The existing
Date.now contract still returns an int wall-clock reading; it does not impose
this calendar range on a host clock binding.

Negative timestamps are supported. Date.toUTC(-1) represents
`1969-12-31T23:59:59.999Z`; subsecond extraction must use floor-based calendar
decomposition, not a negative remainder. Ordinary int arithmetic does not
automatically check the calendar range; each conversion validates its own input.

## Parsing and canonical output

Accept exactly these ASCII shapes:

```text
YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ssZ
YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss.SZ
YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss.SSZ
YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss.SSSZ
```

Each final Z may instead be a numeric offset `+HH:mm` or `-HH:mm`. T and Z are
uppercase; date/time fields have fixed widths. The offset hour is 00..23 and its
minute is 00..59. Positive offsets are subtracted to obtain UTC. Z and +00:00
both specify UTC; -00:00 is rejected because RFC 3339 uses it for an unknown
local offset. Offset syntax does not load or retain a named time zone.

Fractional seconds are optional and, when present, contain one through three
digits, right-padded to milliseconds. A longer fraction is rejected even when
discarded digits would be zero. No truncation or rounding loses input precision.

Reject omitted offsets, date-only or time-only input, whitespace before/after
the input, lowercase separators, expanded/signed/year-zero dates, week/ordinal
dates, comma fractions, leap seconds, end-of-day 24:00, offset seconds, infinity,
embedded NUL, trailing data, and non-ASCII digits. Calendar fields must also
satisfy the preceding range rules. This is a documented subset, not a promise
to parse every ISO 8601 representation or JavaScript Date.parse convention.

Date.toISOString always returns the 24-character ASCII shape
`YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss.SSSZ`, including all three fraction digits and a four-digit
year. It does not depend on locale or machine time zone. For every supported
timestamp t, `Date.parse(Date.toISOString(t)) == t`; reconstructing all fields
from Date.toUTC(t) through Date.fromUTC also returns t. Formatting a parsed input
canonicalizes its offset and precision instead of preserving the original text.

## DateParts

| Read-only property | Type / value |
| --- | --- |
| `parts.year: int` | UTC year |
| `parts.month: int` | UTC month, 1..12 |
| `parts.day: int` | UTC day of month |
| `parts.hour: int` | UTC hour |
| `parts.minute: int` | UTC minute |
| `parts.second: int` | UTC second |
| `parts.millisecond: int` | Millisecond within that second, 0..999 |

DateParts is a fixed-layout standard class with seven int fields, not a Map or
an instant object. Its constructor is not public; Date.toUTC publishes a fully
initialized snapshot. Properties are not writable from Vela code.
It supports ordinary references, nullable annotations, fields, captures,
and typed containers, using the normal class/GC model. Each toUTC call returns
a new instance, and ordinary reference-identity equality applies.

There is no implicit conversion to string, timestamp, Map, or JSON. Persist an
instant explicitly as a timestamp or the result of Date.toISOString. DateParts
does not retain a time zone, native pointer, parser buffer, or reference to
backend calendar objects.

## Errors and allocation

| Failure | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| Invalid parse syntax, field, date, precision, or offset | Error with code `DateParseError` and a clear reason |
| Invalid fromUTC component, out-of-range timestamp, or normalized UTC result | Error with code `DateRangeError`, identifying the component or supported range |
| Wrong static argument, DateParts construction, or property write | Frontend diagnostic; checked builtin calls also validate runtime operands |
| Result/error allocation failure | Existing recoverable OutOfMemory path |

A parse input with valid in-range civil fields and an offset that moves the
UTC result outside the supported range produces DateRangeError. A malformed or
out-of-range input field itself produces DateParseError. Errors are catchable
through ordinary catch/finally, retain source traces, and do not become NaN,
null, zero, a normalized date, or a generic native failure. Human-readable message
wording is not the program-readable contract; Error.code is.

Parsing and field construction return integers and need no result wrapper.
Formatting returns an ordinary immutable string, and toUTC allocates a normal
class instance. Root source strings, arguments, and new results across allocation
safepoints, and publish destinations only after successful completion. A failed
operation does not expose partial strings or objects or modify its inputs.

## Backend and integration

Reuse [Abseil Time](../../third_party/abseil-cpp/absl/time/time.h), already listed
in the [managed build sources](../../third_party/abseil_sources.gni), including
its UTC civil-time conversion and fixed numeric parsing/formatting support.
The new methods perform no zone-database lookup, local-zone discovery, locale
lookup, or clock read. No additional time library is needed.

Enforce the exact ASCII grammar and millisecond precision at the input boundary,
then use Abseil's validated conversion. Its broader ParseTime acceptance of
lowercase separators, arbitrary fractions, leap-second normalization, and
infinite times must not expand this API. For fromUTC, check numeric component
bounds, construct the backend civil value, and compare normalized fields with
the requested fields so an invalid calendar day fails. Range-check the resulting
instant before conversion to int64 milliseconds. Always pass an explicit UTC
zone to formatting; a fixed internal format such as
`%E4Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%E3SZ` supplies canonical field widths. Compute subseconds
relative to the start of the UTC civil second, including for negative timestamps.
Use length-aware parsing, not C-string termination or regex dependencies.

Existing [clock native bindings](../../runtime/library/standard_library.cc) keep their
current responsibilities. Bind the four new conversions through the standard
intrinsic/builtin path so typed DateParts allocation and domain-specific errors
are owned by the shared runtime. The current [native codec](../../runtime/native/native_function.h)
does not return arbitrary class instances; do not introduce an unchecked Value
return or a general object-binding feature for this record. Carry the checked
DateParts class layout from its standard declaration to the runtime consumer
and validate it at compilation/loading, rather than guessing a layout at use.
No new primitive Value kind or calendar object representation is required.

The protected standard environment supplies the checked signatures and
DateParts dependency closure. Standard static methods carry intrinsic markers
through specialization and lowering into ordinary builtin wrapper functions.
LSP, documentation, and source tools consume the same checked signatures.
Method values have fixed full parameter lists; call-site omission supplies
zero defaults for the four optional time fields.

The Isolate owns the canonical DateParts layout. Checked native metadata retains
its standard class role and field shape, and instance creation binds it to that
Isolate. Compiled code and REPL submissions use those runtime layouts.
See [native cache ownership](compilation_cache.md) and
[`examples/time.vela`](../../examples/time.vela).

## Validation

Required regressions cover epoch zero, -1 millisecond, the earliest/latest
supported instants and one millisecond beyond, years below 100, month lengths,
Gregorian century leap rules, every default, named-argument evaluation order,
and all field/type errors. Parsing cases cover each precision, positive/negative
offsets including day/year changes, normalized-range failures, rejected unknown
offset, absent zone, whitespace/NUL/trailing text, excess precision, and leap
seconds. Verify both round-trip identities, DateParts immutability, fresh object
identity, aliased native values, GC/rooting, domain-error propagation and native-instance
reuse, tooling, fresh-Isolate images, and persistent REPL lifetimes. Results must
be invariant under host time-zone and locale changes.

Release benchmarks separately measure parsing, canonical formatting, UTC
construction/decomposition, allocations, and regressions in existing clock
calls. See [measurement boundaries and retained results](../../benchmarks/README.md).

Release benchmarks cover parsing, formatting, fromUTC/toUTC and clocks through
native execution. Keep first-call heap bytes and post-GC retention distinct from
allocation counts and backend storage. Compare only matching suites and
configurations; see [benchmark boundaries](../../benchmarks/README.md).

## References

- [Existing standard declarations](../../compiler/frontend/builtins/standard_environment.cc) and [standard-library time contract](standard_library.md#time).
- [Abseil civil-time types and normalization](../../third_party/abseil-cpp/absl/time/civil_time.h).
- [RFC 3339](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3339), including the unknown-local-offset convention; this API deliberately supports only the stated subset.
- Vela [exceptions](exceptions.md), [source tooling](source_tooling.md), and [compilation cache](compilation_cache.md).

# Source file docs/en/json.md

# JSON and dynamic values

[**English**](json.md) | [简体中文](../zh-CN/json.md)

This document defines the JSON API and checked dynamic value contracts. The runnable
example is [`examples/json.vela`](../../examples/json.vela).

Vela uses Dart's JSON value model: decoding produces ordinary primitive values,
arrays, and ordered maps; encoding accepts those values directly. The public
names are `JSON.parse` and `JSON.stringify`. There is no separate JSON node
class or node-construction API.

```vela
func main(): void {
  const payload: Map<string, dynamic> = {'name': 'Vela', 'items': [1, true, null]};

  const text: string = JSON.stringify(payload);
  const root: dynamic = JSON.parse(text);
  const name: string = root.get('name') ?? '';
  print(name);
}
```

This specification covers in-memory strings, the dynamic type needed by JSON,
and conversion through a public `toJson()` method. It does not add file, stream,
or network I/O; revivers; replacers; conversion callbacks;
or formatting options. [Byte storage and views](byte_data.md) have separate
types and ownership contracts. [Map literals](core_language.md#map-literals)
construct the same native Maps without changing JSON number, null or business
object conversion rules. JSON encoding still requires actual string keys.

## Public API and value model

| API | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| `JSON.parse(source: string): dynamic` | Parse one complete JSON value; return a native Vela value |
| `JSON.parse<T>(source: string): T` | Validate and construct the explicit target type; throw `JSONParseError` for invalid input |
| `JSON.safeParse<T>(source: string): JSONParseResult<T>` | Decode under the same rules; return a failure result for invalid input |
| `JSON.stringify(value: dynamic): string` | Encode a value graph as compact JSON; reject unsupported values and cycles |

`JSON` is a standard static class, available without an import and not
constructible. Its declaration participates in the standard-source dependency
closure and compilation-cache fingerprint, like the existing standard objects.

| JSON value | Decoded Vela value |
| --- | --- |
| `null` | Vela `null` |
| Boolean | `bool` |
| Integer token without a decimal point or exponent | Signed 64-bit `int` |
| Number token containing a decimal point or exponent | `double` |
| String | Immutable UTF-8 `string` |
| Array | `dynamic[]` |
| Object | `Map<string, dynamic>` |

Without type arguments, parse accepts all JSON root types and uses the dynamic model above. Every decoded array uses `dynamic[]`, even
when its current elements are all integers. Object arrays contain maps; parsing
does not construct application class instances. A missing map entry and an
entry containing JSON null both produce null from `get`; use `has` to distinguish
them. Object access uses the existing Map methods, not property-name shorthand.
See [typed JSON decoding](typed_json.md) for generic target types, constructors,
defaults, and structured errors.

## Dynamic typing and checked operations

`dynamic` can hold any Vela value, including null, primitives, enums, instances,
functions, and containers. It is a language type, not a JSON-only wrapper or a
replacement for an invalid frontend type. `void` is not a storable value.
`dynamic` already includes null; an additional `?` is redundant and is rejected.

Assignment to `dynamic` preserves the original value, reference identity, and
language type. Assignment from `dynamic` to a concrete type inserts a runtime
type check. The same rule applies to initialization, assignments, arguments,
returns, fields, indexed writes, and closure captures that cross into a typed
slot. A successful check does not perform numeric conversion or container
conversion. Failure follows the existing checked-cast error path.

The default `implicit_dynamic_conversion` diagnostic warns at implicit boundaries.
Editors publish the same code and severity. This identifies a conversion that may
fail; it cannot predict the contents of runtime JSON. Runtime checks still execute,
and warnings do not prevent compilation.

```vela
const values: dynamic[] = JSON.parse('[7, "Vela", true]');
const id: int = values[0];       // Runtime check succeeds.
const name: string = values[1];  // Runtime check succeeds.
const wrong: int = values[1];    // Catchable checked-cast failure.
```

Member access, method calls, callable invocation, indexing, and operators on a
dynamic receiver are permitted and checked at runtime. Dispatch uses the actual
receiver type and its existing public API. It checks member existence, writable
status, argument names and count, parameter types, and element constraints before
performing the operation. Missing members and invalid operations produce a
catchable type error. Dynamic dispatch cannot access private members, create new
instance fields, or bypass a read-only property. A method obtained as a value
retains its receiver.

Dynamic operations retain Vela's ordinary semantics: integer overflow remains
checked; int/double conversion remains explicit; array bounds remain checked;
and a condition must evaluate to bool. Null-safe operators retain their existing
evaluation order and short-circuit rules. They do not introduce truthiness,
JavaScript coercions, or arbitrary user-defined operators.

`is` and `as` inspect the retained language type. Existing flow refinement
extends to dynamic locals and parameters, and is invalidated by assignments or
calls that can modify captured bindings. Fields and indexed elements are not
promoted. Without a known function signature, a dynamic call cannot provide
context for unannotated lambda parameters; ordinary inference diagnostics apply.
Generic callables must be instantiated before erasure; a dynamic call does not
accept explicit type arguments.

Dynamic typing is introduced by an explicit annotation, a declared dynamic
result, or a dynamic operation. Mixed array literals are allowed in a
`dynamic[]` context; an array literal in a `dynamic` context creates `dynamic[]`.
Absent such a context, existing strict array and return-type inference remains
in force. Unresolved names and inference failures never become dynamic.

Each implicit conversion above warns. An explicit `as` or a valid `is` refinement
expresses the check and does not warn. For example, preserve a null default while
validating every non-null field value:

```vela
const name = (root.get('name') as string?) ?? '';
```

Projects may promote the diagnostic to an error in `vela.json`:

```json
{"diagnostics":{"implicit_dynamic_conversion":"error"}}
```

`"warning"` is also accepted. Source commands and editors search upward from the
entry file's directory for the nearest configuration; without one, warnings are
the default. Test commands use their selected project configuration. Embedding
APIs take `DiagnosticOptions` without implicitly scanning the host filesystem.
Compilation, REPL, and development sessions distinguish warnings from errors;
strict configuration rejects the program before execution. JSON has no provenance
exception, and composite dynamic expressions and nullable targets follow the same rule.

## Containers and business model conversion

Vela containers remain invariant. Storing an `int[]` in a dynamic variable does
not turn its storage into `dynamic[]`. A dynamic call that attempts to insert a
string into that array fails before mutation. Map and Set writes preserve their
declared key/value or element types in the same way.

Conversely, a decoded `dynamic[]` does not become `int[]` just because all its
current elements are integers. Use an explicit checked copy:

```vela
const values: dynamic[] = JSON.parse('[1, 2, 3]');
const integers: int[] = values.map(value => value as int);
```

The map operation is eager. It either returns a new typed array or propagates
the first failed element check. It does not publish a partially filled result.
Existing dynamic objects still need explicit checks and model conversion.
Casting a map to `User` does not instantiate a User. When receiving JSON text,
use `JSON.parse<int[]>(source)` or `JSON.safeParse<User[]>(source)` to validate the
complete target structure and construct actual typed values. See
[typed JSON decoding](typed_json.md).

Dynamic `map` derives the result array's element type from the callback's retained
result signature. Dynamic `reduce` preserves the initial accumulator's actual
type; a null initial value requires a nullable or dynamic accumulator in the
callback signature. Callback contracts are checked even when the array is empty.

Dynamic array elements and dynamic Map/Set slots use tagged storage. Each value
retains the information needed by existing equality and hashing rules, including
enum identity. Existing compact storage for statically typed primitive containers
is preserved. Dynamic keys are supported by ordinary collections; JSON encoding
separately requires every actual object key to be a string.

## Parsing contracts

Parsing accepts the complete JSON value grammar, including heterogeneous arrays.
Only JSON whitespace is accepted around the root. Empty input, extra root values,
trailing garbage, comments, trailing commas, a leading BOM, invalid escapes,
unescaped control characters, and invalid Unicode are errors. UTF-16 escape pairs
are decoded to valid UTF-8; isolated surrogates are rejected. Embedded NUL is
preserved as string content and never terminates a key or value.

Integer tokens must be in `[-2^63, 2^63 - 1]`. Oversized integers are rejected,
including values that a JSON library would otherwise represent as uint64 or
double. Decimal and exponent tokens are converted to binary64 without an
intermediate integer conversion. Finite results use IEEE 754 rounding, including
underflow to signed zero; overflow to infinity is rejected. NaN and infinity
literals are not JSON. Integer `-0` becomes zero; floating negative zero is
preserved.

Object keys are strings. Duplicate keys overwrite the previous value while
retaining the key's original insertion position, following the existing ordered
Map contract. Keys are compared by decoded string contents.

Parsing returns only after the entire input and all numeric and string values
have been validated. Returned strings and containers belong to the Isolate heap;
they do not borrow the input string or a temporary JSON arena.

## Encoding and application objects

Encoding directly supports null, bool, int, finite double, string, arrays, and
maps whose actual keys are all strings. Typed arrays and maps are traversed
directly without converting their whole storage to dynamic containers. Elements
and map values are checked recursively. Enum values are not encoded as their
integer storage. Functions, Set, Future, mutable String, and byte-storage
objects are not directly encodable.

An application class instance is encodable through a public, non-generic,
zero-argument instance method named `toJson`. Its result is processed by the same
encoding rules. The method must return a value. There is no automatic field
reflection, getter enumeration, or conversion based on a class's memory layout.

```vela
class User {
  name: string;
  age: int;

  toJson(): Map<string, dynamic> {
    return {'name': this.name, 'age': this.age};
  }
}

func main(): void {
  const users: User[] = [User(name: 'Vela', age: 7)];
  print(JSON.stringify(users));
}
```

Each occurrence of an object invokes `toJson` once for that occurrence. Exceptions
thrown by the method propagate unchanged through ordinary native frames and retain
their original trace. An unsupported result is an encoding error. Encoding is
synchronous; a Future returned by an async conversion is unsupported.

Cycle detection tracks identities on the current traversal path, including
objects undergoing `toJson` conversion. Returning the receiver from `toJson`, a
container referring to itself, and indirect cycles all fail. Repeated references
in separate branches are legal and are serialized independently.

Traversal uses array order and Map insertion order. Before invoking user code,
the encoder records structural mutation versions for active containers; after
returning, it checks them before using a saved position. A structural change
raises the existing concurrent-modification error, even if the size is restored.
Replacing an existing entry is permitted and is visible if that entry has not yet
been visited. Encoding does not provide a snapshot or roll back user side effects.

Output has no insignificant whitespace or terminal newline. Strings escape
quotes, backslashes, and control characters while retaining other valid UTF-8.
Integers use exact decimal output. Finite doubles use locale-independent shortest
round-trip formatting; output retains a decimal point or exponent so decoding
preserves double kind. Floating negative zero is written as `-0.0`.

## Errors, ownership, and resource use

| Failure | Result |
| --- | --- |
| JSON syntax, Unicode, or numeric-range failure | `Error` with code `JsonDecodeError`; message includes a zero-based UTF-8 byte offset |
| Unsupported encoded value or key, non-finite number, or cycle | `Error` with code `JsonEncodeError`; message identifies the failing value path |
| Dynamic cast, call, member, or index failure | Existing checked-cast, type, or bounds error path |
| Structural mutation during conversion | Existing `ConcurrentModification` path |
| Exception from `toJson` | Original exception and trace |
| Allocation or storage exhaustion | Existing recoverable `OutOfMemory` path |

An unexpected EOF uses the input byte length as its offset. Other decode offsets
refer to the original input, not an unescaped string or modified parser buffer.
JSON-specific error codes must survive builtin/native propagation without being
flattened into a generic native failure. Error-object allocation follows the
existing runtime failure contract when memory is exhausted.

The parser roots partially built containers and values before allocation
safepoints. The encoder roots its input, active containers, conversion receivers,
and conversion results across calls and allocations. Dynamic fields, arrays,
maps, captures, globals, and suspended locals are traced by their actual value
tags; reference publication uses the existing write barrier. JSON temporaries
are released on success and failure, and their external allocations are included
in runtime memory accounting.

Use explicit traversal state rather than unbounded C++ recursion. Complexity is
linear in input/output size plus expected ordered-map operations; duplicate-key
handling must not scan previous keys. Shared graphs may generate repeated output,
so encode cost is measured against output size and conversion work. There is no
language-level fixed nesting limit; resource exhaustion is reported explicitly.

## Implementation and completion

Existing [standard declarations](../../compiler/frontend/builtins/standard_environment.cc),
[builtin signatures](../../compiler/frontend/builtins/builtins.h),
[runtime values](../../runtime/value/value.h), and
[JSON infrastructure](../../base/json.h) establish the integration boundaries.
The existing JSON helper owns yyjson arenas; runtime values must not expose those
nodes. Reuse the pinned yyjson dependency and shared low-level infrastructure.
Preserve raw numeric tokens and original offsets so library numeric coercion
cannot violate the int64 contract. Runtime does not depend on compiler/tooling.

| Stage | Required completion |
| --- | --- |
| Standard environment | Register JSON and its dependent declarations once; preserve reserved names, local shadowing, source overlays, and cache fingerprints |
| Frontend | Add Dynamic; check concrete-boundary conversions, contextual mixed literals, dynamic operations, and refinement invalidation; retain container invariance |
| Runtime identity | Distinguish enums from int, full function signatures, class identities, container arguments, and Future arguments after erasure; reuse canonical type metadata |
| Runtime storage and GC | Add genuine tagged dynamic slots to arrays/collections and trace all dynamic-bearing storage; preserve primitive fast paths |
| IR and compiler | Represent checked conversions and dynamic dispatch explicitly; describe allocations, calls, reads, writes, and throwing effects; preserve evaluation order |
| Native calls and errors | Resolve public members and exact signatures; preserve parse/encode state across ordinary native `toJson` calls |
| Native images and caches | Emit required type and dispatch metadata, bind layouts at instantiation, include metadata in cache identity and reject incompatible native ABIs |
| Tooling | Share checked signatures and dynamic facts with completion, hover, diagnostics, formatting, documentation, debugger, and persistent REPL |
| Delivery | Add `examples/json.vela`, update the feature checklist only after all production paths and required checks pass |

The [offline layout descriptions](../../compiler/ir/layout_description.cc) and
[runtime instantiation](../../runtime/isolate/program_layouts.cc) retain nominal
class, interface and enum identities, structural function signatures,
and Future/Completer payload signatures. Arrays and collections retain their full
element constraints. Boxed enums preserve identity in erased slots while typed
enum arrays retain integer storage. Isolate-owned metadata survives compilation
results; fresh native instances bind the compiled layout descriptions to their Isolate.

Required validation covers all JSON root kinds, heterogeneous and object arrays,
missing versus null entries, duplicate-key order, escaped Unicode and embedded
NUL, int64 endpoints and overflow, binary64 boundaries and signed zero, malformed
input offsets, non-string keys, unsupported types, cycles versus shared branches,
toJson success/failure/mutation, and native-instance reuse after caught errors. Type tests cover
every dynamic-to-typed boundary, private/read-only members, named calls, callable
signatures, enum identity, generic arguments, invariant-container writes, literal
contexts, and invalid inference. GC stress covers partial parsing, conversion
calls, dynamic slots, images loaded in a fresh Isolate, and retained REPL values.

At implementation completion, run relevant Debug/Release regressions, tooling
tests, repository static checks, and Release benchmarks. Measure parse and encode
throughput, allocations and retained memory, dynamic dispatch, typed-boundary
checks, and regressions in ordinary typed code. Completed aggregate measurements
are retained in [the rolling benchmark summary](../../benchmarks/results/rolling_summary.json).
